The primary cause of my leaving mv mother-in-law's house was the fact that I was accused of stealing $5 out of a book which Mrs. Wi'lcox was reading which I saw' my father-in-law deliberately take and put in his pocket. I also swear positively that I maintained my wife and gave her everything she asked for for something like a year and a half after leaving my mother-in-law's house. When taking legal advice I was told by my lawyer to pay my wife no more moneys unless she consented to remove to her own house. ... I received this letter from-them threatening me with proceedings for alimony, and my reply was always that I was willing to support my wife, that the house was still vacant, and that as soon as she moved down with the children I would at once contribute everything necessary for their support. I remained, as near as I recollect, t wo and a half or three years in Port Perry. My wife still refused to move down to her own home. That was before there was any allegation of improper conduct upon wliicli nny relief could be granted In the shape of divorce ; and that evidence goes uncontradicted. The wife listens to it, and does not go into the box and deny it. At the time he offered to take her to her own home and provide for her, as it was his duty to do there was no ground on which she could apply for a severance of the matrimonial fie Again, on page 12 occurs the follou mg evidence with reference to a letter written with regard to alimony : By Mr. Armstrong, for petitioner : Q. We have no such letter or copy of it ?-A. If Mrs. McDermot has my letter she must have it. * When I got that letter from Mrs. McDermot I at once sent her money. I told her I was keeping store in Golden, and told her that everything she required for the children, wearing apparel. I would take great pains in selecting it. I Could buy it cheaper than she could in

Port Perry, and I would be pleased to send anything she asked for. In reply I got a letter back with a long list, something over $165 worth of dry goods, which I filled, and expressed them to Port Perry. I also sent the children a cheque a piece.
That is not denied by the woman ; and this absolutely negatives the allegations as to desertion, cruelty and non-support contained in her evidence-in-chief. Again, on the same page, he says :
I not only did that, but on the next order for goods, as I knew that my wife was a lady who was particularly neat in her appearance and so on-this first time she told me she did not require anything for herself, she was able to provide for herself, but simply wanted goods for the children, but in the same invoice I included several articles of apparel, silk, lace and silk dress for my wife and a quantity of underwear that would come handy, and also a note attached to the goods that in the future she would take everything for herself that I felt like sending. Every request from that day till the present has been complied with. Since that date I have sent a bicycle apiece, snowshoes, watches, each one a watch and chain, and my wife has at different times sent me up orders for goods in the spring of the year that she wished supplied, and I have always supplied them. I also in December, 1904-1 think that is correct-sent my wife two express orders for her own personal use of fifty each.
These allegations are not denied, and the man is taking the risk of his oath, of being convicted of perjury in a very simple manner, because he refers to express orders and express packages of which there is a record. The wife was sitting there and must have heard this evidence as to these remittances and consignments of necessaries ; but she does not say that she never received them and inferentially that he never sent them. Again, on page 13, there is not only the specific denial of the misconduct alleged against him by these women, but there is an explanation of the reason of each of the visits to their house. Now, Sir, these unfortunate women who occupy this class of house have to live, and tradesmen have to go there, to take orders, to deliver goods, and to collect the money in payment for those goods ; and if these people do not pay -and they have not the best credit in the world they have to be looked after, and messengers have to be sent to them. Is any presumption of misconduct to be drawn from the fact that a man in the course of his business does visit these places ? Is he to be branded as a criminal for all time because he does so in the course of bis business as a tradesman ? As is not denied, and as is admitted by the woman in charge of the house, he went there for the purpose of carrying on his business and collecting his debts collecting the money out of which in all probability be sent these remittances to his wife. Is that to be a presumption of guilt against the man, or will this committee require some more tangible or definite to convict him of the charges

made against him ? When under cross-examination, at page 14, he does not abuse his wife. He speaks in the highest terms of her, and he further explains the occasions of the other visits to the woman Harron's house ; and in the whole course of the cross-examination by counsel for the petitioner it is to be observed that the man does not falter from the story he tells. He is subjected to a very close and analytical examination, and his story does not vary generally or in detail; it stands as a straight story, and he is entitled to belief at least as much as the women who acknowledge their own guilt and their own immoral method of livelihood. Granted, then, that his word is as good as theirs, there is no case, because the evidence in favour of innocence, plus the presumption, is greater than the evidence adduced to show guilt. But it is greater, stronger, more reliable, for this reason, that he is definite in regard to the circumstances, he does not vacillate with regard to his facts, and he is not caught, as the women were caught, making statements which are wholly in variance with facts, which they themselves subsequently narrated in the same evidence. There is, in short, the story upon which ibis woman seeks legislative interference to dissolve that which can only be dissolved under our law as it exists at present, by this parliament. My bon. friend from Lincoln has referred in detail to the principles which we must respect in dealing with these Bills. Sir, I must confess that to my mind it is not clear beyond a peradventure that this man was guilty of the charges brought against him, which alone can be the ground upon which this Bill should become law. The relief in a case of this kind is purely discretionary.
There is no right to legislation dissolving the marriage tie, even on specific proof of legal misconduct. It is an application to the state for a privilege to a particular person, it is privilege legislation, legislation in favour of a particular person ; and when we- are dealing with the dissolution of so sacred a tie as the marriage tie, we cannot hedge it about with too many safeguards. And although this Bill might have to be relegated to the committee of the Senate and its further consideration deferred for another session, that would be far better than to judge this man guilty, on the evidence -submitted, of the charges cited in the preamble of this Bill. If there be any doubt in the evidence, who should get the benefit ? All men desire to befriend a woman. That is an obligation laid upon their manhood, but when we come to the question of dissolving a marriage upon charges such as are recited in the preambles of this Bill, it should not matter whether the petitioner be the wife or the husband. We ought to apply the same rule in each case. Let it be established as a principle that this House will reject each and every application for a divorce where

the evidence falls short of proving clearly beyond reasonable doubt the guilt of the respondent, whether man or woman. 1 submit that in the evidence sent down by the Senate there is gTave doubt, doubt so grave that a jury would not hesitate in giving the accused the benefit of it; and I think we might well, if we do uot reject the Bill, send it back to the Senate in order that the matter may be more thoroughly investigated along the lines I have pointed out that no injustice be done.

One would suppose, from the arguments advanced by the hon. members for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) and Algoma (Mr. Boyce), that this Bill is an entirely novel proceeding and one that has never been brought before the House since confederation. As a matter of fact, however, these Bills for absolute divorce or dissolution of the vinsulum matrimonii have been granted from time to time since confederation ; and if we follow the English precedent we can go back as far as 1551 to find the oldest case on record in England in which the principle of divorce has been acted upon. And so long as persons bring themselves within certain recognized principles, it has been the custom of parliament, and in later years in England and in some portions of this Dominion it has been the power likewise of the courts, to grant these Bills of divorce. Every one knows that there are certain elementary principles which must govern in divorce cases and which must be complied with before divorces are granted. This is not simply, as has been stated in the House, an action between two. parties. It is an action in which a third party is interested. It is the duty of the state to see that no injustice is done, it is the duty of the state to protect society, but it is also its duty, when specific charges are proved, to mete out the same measure of justice to one party that is meted out to another. In the first place, the petitioner must come into court with clean hands. There must be no crime or guilt on his part. Has there been in this case the least attempt to prove any unbecoming conduct on the part of the petitioner ? We have the evidence before us. The witnesses were brought before the Senate committee. The respondent had every chance to bring witnesses, and to my mind what has stronger weight than anything else, we have the testimony of an hon. member of this House, who represents the riding in which the petitioner lives, and who says that no more virtuous woman lives in the province of Ontario. Therefore the first, and to my mind, one of the most important elements has been settled. The next important element is that there must, be no collusion between the parties. Surely no one will conclude that in this case there has been any. Then the next-question is whether the ordinary cause of divorce has been proven. The hon. gentlemen who have addressed this House asked us to go back to the principle adopted by the English parliament prior to 1857 and by the English courts to a very large extent since and that is to grant to the husband a right they will not grant the wife. I do not think that such was the intention of parliament. True these hon. gentlemen did not say so in terms, but I can draw no other inference from the arguments they advanced.
I said just the opposite.
I submit that it is a reasonable deduction to draw from the remarks of these hon. gentlemen that we should withhold from the woman the right we are willing to grant the man.
Not at all. Neither of us took that ground.

I am glad my hon. friends say they took grounds quite the opposite. That removes one very grave doubt I possessed. But if they have any doubt about the principles to be followed in the Canadian House, all they need do is read the famous Tudor-Hartt case decided in 1888 and they will conclude that the English law has not been followed in Canada, and I hope never will. I know of no more mischievous and unfair legislation than to deny to the woman the right to a divorce which would be granted the husband.
Hear, hear.

That brings me to the question whether or not the charge made against this man has been proven. It is not a question whether the wife deserted her husband or whether he deserted her, because desertion, no matter how cruel or under what extraordinary circumstances, is not in Canada-and I hope never will be-a ground for divorce. I shall not go over all the nauseating evidence given before the Senate committee, but I do submit that according to the evidence, the case of the petitioner has been proven beyond doubt. We are told that we ought not to take the evidence of the two women brought from British Columbia. Why ? Because they are prostitutes forsooth.
Did the hon. gentlemen who are opposed to this Bill expect to find evidence of .this kind except in houses of prostitution ? Do you go to the drawing-rooms or the higher classes of society for such evidence ? Do you go to our churches or our schools for evidence of thisi kind ? If these hon. gentlemen had ever practised in the divorce courts or had had experience of this sort of legal matters elsewhere, they would know that you must go to these places to get this kind of evidence. And they would know that case after case in Canada has been decided within the last fifty years on evidence such as this. In the province of New Brunswick they have a divorce court. And I submit that it is as hard to

get a divorce before the courts of New Brunswick as before this parliament of Canada, if not harder. Nine months ago I listened to a ease in that court in which a divorce was granted and the only evidence given was brought from a house of ill-fame as in this case. The judge in that case-it is usual for the cases to be tried by a judge alone, though lie can have a jury under certain circumstances-had no difficulty in coming to the conclusion that the case had been proved.
Mr. BOYCiE. Was there no corroborative evidence ?
Mr. iQAElVEIiL. There certainly was and it was just such evidence as we have in this case showing that this man had been seen frequenting these places. And you do not want better corroboration. You do not get direct evidence in these cases- and it is a good thing you do not. I would refer my hon. friends to a case showing the rule of evidence adopted in these matters. For, Sir, as I have said before, we do not get the direct evidence in these cases and are compelled to rely on circumstantial evidence. I do not believe there is one such case in twenty-five decided in this House or in the courts of this country, but the evidence is largely circumstantial. I would refer these hon. gentlemen to the diction of Lord Stowell in the Lovedon case case in the House of Lords, about the year 1832. I cite from Gemmill on Divorce, page 206 :
It is a fundamental rule that it is not necessary to prove the direct fact of adultery ; because if it were otherwise, there is not one case in a hundred in which the proof would be attainable. In every case almost, the fact is inferred from circumstances that lead to it by fair inference as a necessary conclusion.
INow, X will not refer to the evidence of these women at all. I think it highly im-piioper to refer to that evidence in this House and put it on ' Hansard.' I ask members of this committee to refer to that evidence of which each hon. member has received a copy. You have absolute evidence of this woman who is seeking a divorce, and you have it denied iu toto, almost in toto, by the defendent himself. But there is another important matter which we must 'consider, and that is that the members of this committee have not had the privilege which is granted in every other court 'I have ever heard of, namely Ithat those who are to decide as to the weight of evidence, must see the witnesses on the stand that they may watch their demeanour, and judge by their manner and *appearance Whether they are or are not worthy of credence. This House has not had that privilege. But in the Senate committee they have had that privilege. And [DOT]the members of that .committee and the many members of the Senate who have unanimously decided in favour of passing Mr. CARVELL.
this Bill are in an infinitely better position to decide upon this case than the members of this committee who have only the bald facts reported to them. These women tome and give their evidence. And because they are women of ill-repute their evidence, we are told ought not to be taken. J made it my- business to go to members of the 'Senate, and .they told me that these women gave their evidence with the utmost difidence, that it was almost impossible to drag that evidence out of them, and that it was evident .from their actions that they, were telling the truth, that they had been brought here against their will and were forced to give evidence. But we iu this House do not know anything about that. All we know is that these witnesses swore to these things, and that the defendant denied them. There is another important matter. If I lvad read tbe evidence of the husband alone and bad not read the evidence of the petitioner or the petitioner's witnesses, merely from the way the defendant gave his evidence, I would say that it was about as hard a piece of evidence to believe as I ever heard of. The man has double tbe assurance of those ha/rlots who have been held up in such an unfavourable light here to-night. Take the man's evidence as it stands and he denies his marriage, ddniesi that they lived together as husband and wife, denies that they bad three children. Probably this was not bis intention. But he specifically and categorically denies certain charges made against him by the wife in her examination, charges that are sworn to toy two other witnesses, ilt is impossible for Mm to deny that he was a frequent visitor at the house of the women Han-on and Clarke. He tells us that it was necessary to go there in the course of his business to sell goods to these women. Had he stopped there, he might have been entitled to credence. But he does not stop there. He says he went there to introduce commercial travellers. What for ? That they might also sell these women goods. And'he tells us in the next breath that he sold nearly, ail the silk goods sold in the town of Golden and that, these "women were the prim [DOT]eipal purchasers of these goods-. When a man makes his livelihood by selling good$ to womdn of this kind and then telis us that he took commercial travellers to sell goods in direct competition with himself and prevent liim from making a profit, the evidence is hard to believe. ,But that is his explanation of why he entered those houses of ilMame. That alone should toe enough 'to convince (any? honest man that this-witness is-I will not use as harsh a word as perjurer, but is not entitled to the credence which would deny this woman the right to divorce if this committee believe that in any case husband and wife should be divorced.
'Now. there lias been a good deal said

about whether or not this man deserted his wife, or whether his wife deserted him. As I said before, so far as the crucial point is concerned, it matters not to me which it Was. il think there will be a lot' of evidence found to show whether this man is worthy of belief or not. One thing is very certain-he only provided a home for his wife for about six months after he was married, and them because he could not provide a home or did not want to do so, they went to her father's house and remained there for five or six years, after which he left. A great deal was said about his not being able to get along with his father-in-law and mother-in-law, and he tries to make out that it was never his fault. But he gives Dire lie to his statement from beginning to end because he admits that in one month after he left his mother-in-law's house he made an arrangement by Which he gave his wife $12.50 a month and carried on this arrangement for a year. Is that consistent with the idea that he left because lie could not get along with his [DOT]wife's parents and was pleading with his wife to leave ? Why should he put her off with a pension of $12X0 a month ? If he wished to keep her with him would he not have given her everything he could ? But he gets rid of tier in the easiest way he can. He gives her $12.50 a month and says ; Take that, for it is all you will get. And this arrangement he continued for a year or fifteen months. He lives there in the same village for two years after this ; not one dollar of support does she get from him and finally after about three years he goes west and becomes, 'as he says himself, a Lothario. He admits it); not only admits it, but glories in it. He is what is described in the dictionaries as a gay deceiver, a libertine, a man w:tbout character, a man who glories in the fact that lie sets at defiance the laws of God as well as of man.
I do not know how it struck my hon. friend but I know I noticed the same expression in the evidence and it struck me that he did not understand the expression.

If my hon. friend can point to anything in the evidence which shows- that he did not understand the expression. X have not been able to see it, The evidence is simply that the counsel for the petitioner asks :
You were rather a Lothario in the west ?
And he answers :
Yes.
That is all there is to it, and I would like to know bow on earth my hon. friend can read into this language the fact that he did not understand the expression. I do not think the respondent will thank him for saying there is anything on earth he does
not understand. If you read the evidence you will come to the conclusion that in his own mind he knows everything there is on this earth and a little of what is in the next world as well. We have this man on his own admission a gay deceiver, a libertine, a man who glories in it and who goes out there and is certainly a frequenter of these houses of ill-fame. He lives there for eight or ten years and there is not a particle of evidence that lie ever offered to contribute one dollar to his wife's support, until some two or three years ago when she wrote, and then he would not give a cent until she signed a statement that it was not to be taken as a precedent that he would not be liabaie for alimony. Then she sent a list of goods which she needed for her children. He tries to make a virtue of necessity by claiming that after proceedings had been started, not after the subpoenas had been issued, but after he knew that an attempt was to he made to bring the matter before the Senate of Canada, then he becomes magnanimous and then without being solicited he sends presents to the children and express orders to his wife and she returns them. If there is anything in this evidence for which I admire this woman, il is the fact that wthen the matter had gone to the extent it had she had the womanhood to return the money by which lie was trying to buy peace.
We now come down to the last matter which I propose to mention in reference to the question whether this woman or this man should be believed and it is this. We have the evidence of the man himself that he left this woman some five or six years after their marriage, in 1889, and that in all the sixteen years intervening he has not contributed more than $400 to her support ; he admits it himself. We have the evidence, as I said before, that he has led a wild, dissolute life in the west, that he has inhabited houses of ill-fame. 1 am taking his own admission, not the evidence of these women, and when his wife swore to the most abominable piece of evidence I ever listened to by a wife, which will be found at page 2 of the evidence, X say the man did not deny it. It seems almost too inhuman to he placed in print, it seems so bad that you can hardly believe that a man living in a Christian country would sink so low, to such a depth of degradation, that he would treat a woman as this woman was treated by him-and that at a time when he was professing to live with her as her husband. She swears at liage - .
I was in child-birth and I asked Mm to go for the doctor, and he refused positively and swore at me and said : damn it all why didn't I tell him before it was time to retire ?
I submit that has not been denied. In the first paragraph of his evidence he denied categorically the facts that he had thrown the children under the table, bent their fingers back and driven her out of the

house. He denied these charges, but he has not denied this charge.
What does my hon. friend say of the fact that the woman forgave him for that and lived with him for several years after ? Is that not an answer.

I am not asking the committee to pass the Bill on that evidence. I am asking the committee to believe that this man is not worthy of belief, a man who is brutal enough to make a remark of that kind under those circumstances is not fit to be believed in any court in any Christain or civilized country, and that a man who is sufficiently mean to do that is one of the most despicable specimens of humanity that it has ever been my experience not only to meet but to read of. With this evidence I have no hesitation in coming to the conclusion that the man has been proven guilty of adultery, and therefore, as I read the law, a divorce should be granted. But that raises another question. The hon. gentlemen who are opposing the passage of this Bill seem to be advocating something which so far as I have been able to read has never been advocated in this House since 1888 and I know not how long before that time. I may be in error but I have inquired from older members and I have been unable to find a single instance from 1888 when this House has ever questioned the finding of the Senate on this matter of divorce. Why has that rule been followed ? Simply because an agreement was made. In the first place they are following the custom of the House of Lords of England, a custom which prevailed in England from 1551 down to 1858 when these matters were handed over to the divorce court. Then in the old province of Canada these matters were taken up by the legislative council and after confederation was consummated these matters were taken into consideration by the Senate and have been ever since. Under the customs and rules of the Senate passed in 1888 and even before that, they have had the power, and have exercised that power, of (bringing before them the witnesses, the witnesses give their evidence viva voce as in all courts of law and the committee of the Senate who have listened to the witnesses, watched their demeanour, observed the manner in which they give their evidence, forming their conclusion more I say from watching the manner of the witnesses than the actual evidence, these Senate committees have been passing these questions and their decision has been taken as final by this House as far back as 1888.
Why then do they ever come before this chamber ?
Because under our present system of legislation it is necessary that a Bill be passed by both Houses of parliament.
Hear, hear.

If we are considering the evidence then I say we should be manly about it, I say that we should pass this Bill and give notice to the people of Canada that in future every divorce Bill is going to be contested in the House of Commons as well as in the Senate. Suppose this rule had existed in this case what would have been done ? These witnesses would have been brought before either the Private Bills Committee or a special select committee to give evidence, and members of this House would have had the privilege of going into that committee and listening to these people giving i their evidence. Members of this House would have been treated as a jury is treated in a court of law, and would have been in a position to decide upon this matter intelligently on the principles of their common sense and their judgment, and they would not have been compelled to take the evidence second-hand as we are compelled to do in this case. I submit that this parliament has never adopted that principle. Let us be fair and manly about it, let us give the people of the Dominion of Canada public notice of it and let us put people in such a position that they will not leave a case half tried when they have got through with the Senate. These witnesses I presume have gone back to British Columbia. We have no way of getting their testimony or finding out whether they have sworn the truth or not. We must simply take the evidence as it was produced before the Senate. It is not fair; this woman or her friends have been compelled to put up I suppose $500 or $1,000 in order to get this case in the position it is to-night, and now in an unfair and unusual manner, in a manner which I admit the House has a legal right to adopt but which has not been employed for fifteen years, it is attempted to hold up this Bill simply because we have not this evidence before us.
Another peculiar course was taken on Friday evening by the two learned gentlemen who have discussed this case here tonight. Then a different line of action was taken. On that occasion we were asked to submit this matter to the Minister of Justice. Think of it! When the hon. member for Centre York (Mr. Campbell) asked the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) why he wanted to submit it to the Minister of Justice, he said that he wanted to get a legal decision ; and when asked what legal decision, he said that he wanted to know whether or not there was sufficient ground on which to grant this divorce.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) is making my speech for me.

Am I ? I will do my hon. friend the justice of reading from the record, which, I presume, he will not deny, and I will leave it to the committee to decide

whether or not I have properly quoted him. I read from the unrevised edition of ' Ham sard ' of Friday, May 19, at page 6511:
Mr. CAMPBELL,. Now I think that this is a childish, I think it is frivolous, the most frivolous argument ever advanced in this House for a man of the ability of the 'non. member for Lincoln, or the hon. member for Algoma, to seriously propose to refer this to the Minister of Justice for a judicial decision upon the legal point. What legal point is there about it ?
The legal point is whether the evidence here is legally sufficient to warrant the stain of guilt that is sought to be put on this man.
Who is to decide that ?

Is that not a proper question for the law officers of the Crown to decide?
I ask is there a lawyer in this House who ever heard such a proposition as that ?
Does my hon. friend deny that that would not be a proper course ?
I most certainly deny that it is a proper course.
Well, then, my hon. friend is not acquainted with the rules of the Senate.

I will read rule * O ' of the Senate, and we will see what that rule says. I want to treat the hon. gentleman fairly, I want to give him all the evidence and the law I can on the question, and while I do not hope to convince the hon. gentleman, yet, Sir, I will try to make my own position tenable before the committee Rule 'O' is as follows :
Condonation, collusion or connivance between the parties is always a sufficient ground for rejecting a Bill of divorce, and shall be inquired into by the committee. And should the committee have reason to suspect collusion or connivance and deem it desirable that fuller inquiries should be made, the same shall be communicated to the Minister of Justice, that he may intervene and oppose the Bill should the interest of public justice in his opinion call for such intervention.
Does the hon. gentleman contend that the House of Commons has not the same right to invoke that as the other chamber as to the necessity for passing this Act ?

I am willing to admit that it is only a fair inference that the House of Commons shall have the same right to invoke the opinion of the Minister of Justice on these points as the Senate, but when hon. gentlemen ask us to refer this question to the Minister of Justice in order to decide whether there has been condonation or collusion, I say away with such an idea. Where is the evidence of condonation ? I ask the hon. member for Lincoln and the hon. member for Algoma to point out where there is collusion in this case. They have talked about collusion between the wife and these women from British Columbia. They have even gone so far as to
I think the hon. gentleman is going beyond the mark.

They have even gone so far as to talk of collusion between the wife and these women from British Columbia. That is not the meaning of collusion. Collusion, as it is used in that rule, and as it is understood in law, means an agreement or arrangement between the husband and wife by which a divorce might be brought about which otherwise would not be brought about. Where is the evidence of any legal collusion in this case ? What is there to submit to the Minister of Justice on the question of collusion ? Then, the next thing that is mentioned is connivance. Connivance in law means that if one party, husband or wife, intentionally places either one in a position that the statutory charge may be preferred against either, they are not entitled to any redress in this House or before a court of law. Where is the evidence of connivance ? Do they claim that because this woman, after being treated as she was, would not go with this man because he went off to British Columbia and associated with harlots, is responsible for his association with these women ? Do they claim that she drove him into these wrongful acts ? That is the only logical conclusion they can arrive at, that is the only way they can make out that there is any connivance ; and if there is any connivance, what do they want to submit to the Minister of Justice ? Do they want the Minister of Justice to tell them that this parliament has power to pass a divorce Bill ? Do they want the Minister of Justice to tell them, as a lawyer, that if they believe the evidence of these two women, they are justified in finding the charge proven, and -that the Bill should pass ? Or do they want to put this thing off in order to get rid of a vote upon the matter ? If so, I say they are giving us a childish pretext for asking the Minister of Justice to decide upon the whole case.
That is pretty hard on the Minister of Justice.

It is pretty hard on the Minister of Justice; I thought so when I listened to it. I thought that surely these hon. gentlemen knew the law. I do not think the hon. member for Lincoln will plead guilty to ignorance of the _law and I am absolutely certain that the hon. member for Algoma will not plead ignorance of the law. There is no question about that. I wonder at them wanting the Minister of Justice to go over the evidence, to come down here and take the place of the jury, take the place which has been occupied by laymen since the time of Magna Charta, and to decide according to this evidence if this man is guilty or not. I have taken up much more time in discussing this case than I intended to, but I do submit that this parliament, in the first

place under the British North America Act, has power to grant this divorce. This parliament fifteen or twenty years ago adopted the principle of allowing the evidence to be presented before a Senate committee. The Senate committee and the Senate itself, after passing upon these cases, send them, dowm here and the recommendations of the Senate have invariably been concurred in. If this House is going to change that principle then I say the only proper thing for us to do is to pass this Bill. If we believe that this man is guilty of adultery, and I do not think there are half a dozen hon. gentlemen in this House who do not believe in their hearts that he is guilty of adultery, then I say we should pass this; Bill. If this House desires that a different principle should be followed in future let us adopt that principle, make it public and let everybody who wishes know the principle upon which these matters are going to be decided, let them give their evidence before the Senate, then bring their evidence over here, before a committee of this House and then we will be able to decide intelligently, but until that plain intimation is given to the people of this country, I submit that if this man is guilty of adultery; it is the bounden duty of this House to pass; this Bill and let this woman have her divorce. There is only one other observation that I desire to make. The hon. member for Lincoln undertook to play upon the sympathies and credibility of the members of this House by asking us if the case were reversed and two bad men attempted to. swear away the rights of an innocent wo-! man whether every man here would nof stand up and say :	We shall not believe',
such evidence, we shairnot give credence to it. But, he left out the important part ofi the argument. Let any woman come into this House and admit, as this man admits that she has been living with harlots for the last ten years of her life, let' any woman come into this House and admit that she has been living the life that he admits he has been living, and I ask. if there is a man In this committee, if there is a member of this parliament, if there is a legal gentleman or a Christian gentleman in Canada who would not say that this woman ought to be divorced and who would not grant a divorce without discussing it for two minutes. I say that there has been no case ma'de out against this woman, but that on the other hand there has been a strong and absolutely unanswerable case made out by the woman against the husband, and for that reason I contend the Bill should pass.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) has not referred to the main argument I made, namely : what is the interest of the country in this matter? Would the hon. gentleman tell me what good he thinks it would do the country to pass this Bill ?

My answer is this: for the past 3<XI years it has been the settled policy of the parliament of Great Britain to grant divorce when adultery has been proved against the woman. In 1832, the parliament of Great Britain granted a divorce for the adultery of the husband, Tlie rule was laid down positively and absolutely by tliis House in tlie Tudor and Hart case in 1888 that adultery, unaccompanied by an unnatural crime is, as required in England, sufficient ground for divegee by the wife. If this House is convinced that the charge has been proven against the husband then it is our right beyond a question to grant the divorce, and I submit, following the practise, it is our duty to pass this Bill and grant this wife a divorce.
I do not yet quite understand from the hon. gentleman what good purpose is served in the country by encouraging divorce on such evidence as has been produced in this case.

My only answer is this: if the hon. gentleman wishes to take the position which a large and influential body in Canada take, namely, that he is unalterably opposed to divorce, then I can understand bim.
I am opposed to divorce except in extreme cases.
If he admits that divorce is proper in extreme cases, then as this is an extreme case, and on the ground of public policy he should support the Bill.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will the Minister of the Interior please explain what this large sum is required for ?

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This rote is asked to complete the immigration services for the year. The sum originally quoted was $672,276. The expenditures for several years have overrun the estimates. It is found impossible in practice to estimate closely the immigration expenditures from the fact that as the flow of immigration increases the expenses increase proportionately ; that is to Say the increase in expenses in one year is dependent upon the success of the operations of the preceding year. If the estimate for the coming year is based only on the estimate made for the present year the immigration efforts of the past year have been successful in securing an increased immigration. naturally the estimates for the current year fall short. That has occurred in this case to a serious degree. Besides, provision was not made in last year's estimates for the shortage of the previous year and this lias to be provided for as well as the increased expenditure, because of tbe increased immigration.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If tbe bon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) will turn up ' Hansard ' he will find that last year when Mr. Sifton was putting through his estimates he described a state of affairs quite different from that described by tlie present minister.
What would be the total cost for immigration last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Does that include salaries and everything ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Everything.
I understand tbe minister to say that this is to provide for the increased immigration this year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
ill-. URIAH WILSON. This is a very large increase and there was also a large increase last year over the previous year. How many immigrants came in for the last *ten months ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot for the moment give the actual figures, but the estimate of the total immigration for the current fiscal year is : British immigrants, 67,548; French and Belgian, 2,572 ; other continental countries, 33.486 ; United States, 44,055 ; total, 148,261, as against 130,000 last year.

I went to the trouble to send down to Mr. Scott tile other day for some information when I saw that this vote of $300,000 extra was asked for. I have the statement of Mr. Scott in my hand and it shows that the total immigration during the the ten months. July 1, 1904, to April 30, 1905, was : ocean ports, 67,808 ; United States, 31,969 ; total, 99,777. If we got the same average number of immigrants for the next two months there would he only 120,000 compared with 130,000 last year. The previous year we spent $744,788, which was a very large expenditure ; this year the main estimates contained an appropriation of $672,270 and now $300,000 is asked making $972,276, while according to this report the immigration will he less than last year. To have it as large as last year it would he necessary to get at least 30,000 immigrants in the next two months. It does seem to me that this increased expenditure is entirely unjustifiable, and unless the minister can give some better reason than he has given the item should not pass. Of course,-if the money has been spent we may have to pay it, but there should be some satisfactory reason given why we should spend nearly $1,000,000 a year on immigration when our immigration system is now so well established. Long before this government came to power we had our immigration agents in the United States and the policy was initiated. It is well known all over this continent and pretty well known irf Europe, that we have the best wheat producing field in the world, and that we are giving every immigrant 160 acres free of any charge except a fee of $10 for the patent. It does seem to me that this ought be sufficient inducement, and that in the future we ought not to increase our expenditure every year. When you get a business well established and in good running order that ought be sufficient without increasing your outlay. I quite understand the difficulty the minister is in, seeing he is not long in office, and that while out of office he was not much in sympathy with the manner in which the business was carried on. He is not responsible for the expenditure up to the present time, but some minister who has been in charge of the departments since Mr. Sifton retired ought to he able to give the committee a reason why this additional sum should be voted. I may say that I also asked Mr. Scott to give a statement of the expenditure up to the present time, but he does not seem to have been able to do so. He says :
Expenditure for immigration by Mr. Preston, July 1st, 1904, to February 28th, 1905 ; by Mr. Smith from March 31st, 1905 ; at Ottawa to May 16th, 1905 ; total, $6)21,206.38.
This does not tell how much has been spent altogether and I can see no good reason why there should be an unsettled account in the old country from February 28 to the present time. The minister ought be able to give us the expenditure in the old country, in the United States and in Canada up to date.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As I have said the increase is partly accounted for by increased ex-

penditure occasioned by the increased flow of immigrants, and partly by reason of part of tlie expenditure of last year being carried over to this year.
Tell usi how much has been carried over.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am making the general statement. I can give a particularised statement of the expenditure.

I think it would be well to let this item stand until the hon. minister can get the full information. I would also like to know whether the department have largely increased their staff ? if they have, what was their reason for doing so, where it is increased, and what the duties of the additional officers are ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Three new agencies have been opened in the United States-at Syracuse, New York ; at Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and Boston. There has also been an increase of effort in Great Britain. There has been no increase on the continent. I am able to give particulars of the disiposi-tion that has -been made of the vote in the main estimates, and also of the disposition proposed to be made of the amount asked for to-night, if the House would care to have them.
We would like to have them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The expenditures that have been made out of the sums voted last session for the year ending the 30tli of June, 1905, are as follows :-Contingencies in Canada generally, including salaries and expenses of Messrs. Hillyard, Heboe, Johnston, Charlebois, White, Ross and Ward, and expenses of Messrs. Smart, Scott, Speers, &c., .$8,850.69 ; contingencies and general expenses of United States agencies, including salaries of temporary agencies. $40,384.27; King's Printer's accounts, $1,531.72; telegrams, freight and express charges, $2,980.58 ; salaries of extra clerks, head office, $4,847.55; medical services and expenses, including salaries and expenses of doctors, not including detention hospital, $5,217.15 ; grants to detention hospitals at Halifax, Quebec and 'St. John, services, supplies, Sec., $7,643.16 ; grants to hospitals, $2,301.12 ; commissions on settlers from the United States, $3,399.25 ; seaport expenses, Halifax, St. John, Quebec and Montreal, $5,135.59 ; uniforms, seaport agencies, head office, $1,639.14 ; postage, $4,235.79 ; Quebec and Lake St. John Railway, $8,000 ; Quebec and Lake St. John Repatriation and Colonization Society, $3,000 ; La Soeiete de Repatriation et Colonization de Quebec, $1,200 ; Immigration Association of Western Canada, $2,500 ; Ottawa Valley Immigration Aid Society, $750 ; motor van, $1,250 ; miscellaneous expenses, $4,158.75.
Who uses the automobile ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is for the purpose of bringing the exhibits of Canadian farm products into the agricultural parts of the old country, which it is difficult to reach by railway. It is an automobile of high horsepower, upon which is constructed a van containing specimens of the agricultural products of the west, and it is managed by two men, who run it from village to village and give exhibitions. Commissioner Smith's expenses, which are for the purpose of placing immigrants, as distinguished from the expenditure for inducing immigrants to come, amount to $86,873.54 ; contingencies and general expenses of agencies in (Jr eat Britain and Ireland and on the continent, $36,605.48 ; British bonuses, as estimated by Mr, Preston, $201.
What is meant bv these ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are bonuses paid to the steamship agencies to induce them to direct immigration to Canada. The Women's National Immigration Society, $500 ; Girl's Home of Welcome, $500 ; tents for Barr colonists, balance of account. $18,900.
Can the minister tell us what the tents cost altogether ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: About $32,000 altogether.
Where were these tents obtained ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: From the Militia Department.
Were they obtained by tender ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They were taken over from the Militia Department.
These were not new tents, and surely you do not pay full price for old tents almost useless.
The Barr colonists claim that the tents were absolutely useless. What prices were paid ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The price was about $25 each for Bell tents, about 12 feet in diameter. They had been in use by the Militia Department. The colony came out very early in the season, and it was absolutely necessary they should be provided with shelter in some way. It was impossible to procure such a large number of tents from any other source. It was a matter of urgency, the tents were procured and had to be paid for.
Were they just tents that were abandoned by the Militia Department ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They were tents in use by that department.

Had the Militia Department to purchase new tents ?
Mr: OLIVER. Certainly. They were used by the Immigration Department, and those
still useful are available for us. Those not in use are stored in Winnipeg.

Does the hon. gentleman really know how many of them are stored or what became of these tents V Let us have the whole story ? Let the minister himself find out what the tents cost and at what prices, what other firms would tender for the making of them, how many were used by the Barr colonists, and where they are now.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman requests that information, I must provide it. But I do not think it has any material bearing on the case. It was urgent that these people should be provided with shelter, and whether the price was high or low was a secondary consideration. The immigrants could not be left to suffer.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The government had in their possession all these tents and all they had to do was to borrow them from the Militia Department and they could be returned when no longer required. There was uo necessity why the immigrants should suffer so long as the government had a large quantity stored up and there was no need to replace them at a price far above what they could be purchased for at public tender.

How many immigrants came out in that Barr colony ?
Mr. OLIVER As the Barr colony came out two years ago, I presume the information has already been before the House, but I can get it again if necessary.
How many immigrants are now being detained at Montreal ? I understand that a large number are detained there and are to be deported. Has the minister any information about that ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not heard about it but can get information.

I suppose this money is about expended, and I would be willing to let this go through on the understanding that we will have a perfect right to discuss these things and have the oflicials of the Immigration Department appear before the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization. Comparatively little has been done before that committee this year for several reasons, and we ought to have an investigation before the main estimates are passed for the coming year. I know something of the history of the hon. minister in the past and his views with reference to immigration! and I trust we are entering upon a different era in that respect. I think that the amount we are spending this year, something like a million dollars, is altogether out of proportion to the work being done, and some two years ago the hon. minister was of the same opinion. Now that he occupies a position where he can control to a large extent this department, I
trust he will not call on us to spend nearly a million; dollars for immigration next year. Such an expenditure is altogether unnecessary. Our country is becoming tolerably well known, and while I would not be willing to abandon the field, I think our expenditure should be kept within reasonable bounds, more especially as our neighbours are not spending a dollar on immigration except for the purpose of keeping undesirable immigrants out of their country. I am afraid, from information I .have, that if we continue our course, we shall have in the near future to take similar precautions. We do not only require immigrants to be carefully examined on this side, but they ought to be examined before being allowed to go on board ship. From what I have read in the American press, the American vessels are frequently loaded with the best immigrants-those who would pass an examination-and the undesirable ones are put on board ship for Canada. That accounts for the few the Americans have to reject at their ports and for the large number they reject when	they come to
Canada." With this understanding I should be quite willing to let the item go through because I know we need the money ; but before the main estimates go through for the coming year, we ought to have a full investigation before the committee, and the minister should give us a full account of all he intends to do with the money as well as some explanation of what has passed.
Mi-. OLIVER. I shall be glad to do so. My desire is to give the House the fullest possible information. Aid I may say that the information in my hands is pretty full, but, of course, these questions can be discussed to better advantage before the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization than in the House. So, I can promise the hon. member (Mr. Uriah Wilson) that, what ever may 'be the result in the Committee of the Whole he certainly shall have the fullest opportunity before the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization to discuss all matters of policy and administiation m regard to immigration.

It is matters of detail that we want in that committee, and the permanent officers of the department ought to be in better position to give these details than the minister. And we want these men before the committee.
Mi-. OLIVER. I will guarantee that they will furnish ail the details. I have many details here which I shall he glad to give.
HUGHO0S. Has the minister a comparative statement showing the number of immigrants' coming in month by month this year and last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have the record of these coming year by year.
Has the minister the number comiaig in since the opening of navigation ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I have not that information here. The hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson) suggested that the number arriving in the first ten months of this year was not as large in proportion as the number arriving last year. The point I wished to make was that it is in ihe remaining months of the year that we expect the large immigration.
What does the minister estimate the immigration to be from the 30th of April to the 30th of June ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think thait the figures that the hon. member (Mr. Uriah Wilson) lias and those that I have will enable us to arrive at it What do the figures he has show ?

They show the number arriving up to 30th -April-ocean ports 66,880 ; United States, 31,969 ; total, 99,849.
Mr. -OLIVER. My estimate of the whole wtas 148,261.
What I wanted was the estimate for the two months from 30th April to 30th June.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: That is an enormous estimate, is it not ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These are the months of large immigration. The immigration movement in winter, both from Europe and the United States, is small. I am not altogether familiar with the working of the department, but I am -satisfied that the great bulk of our immigration is in. the months of spring and early summer.

I would like the minister to instruct his officers to give the number of immigrants for the last three weeks- that is, from April 30th to May 21st. Then, there will only be five or six weeks of the year to come and we should he able to form a better idea of the total immigration and' judge what the results of this increased expenditure has been.

It seems to me we cannot impress upon the new minister too strongly the importance of being careful about the immigrants admitted to this country, for it is well known that the new comers may prove a curse rather than a blessing. We have to face the fact that the charitable institutions from one end of the Dominion to the other complain that a number of the immigrants brought into Canada have become a burden upon them. I can scarcely understand how it is that we have to deP irt such a large number if there is a careful medical examination made before the im-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: migrants leave the ports whence -they come. Last year we had an immigration of 134,000 adults and 17,000 children under 12 years of age. We paid for medical ser-vince over $54,000. Yet, we find that a large number of these immigrants are suffering from diseases which it makes it necessary to deport them. ,So far as the instructions given by the minister are concerned, they seem to be very good, buit those instructions can hardly ibe carried out or the results would be better. It must be that many of the agents, anxious to swell the number work in m-any who are not desirable immigrants- for this country.

I understand that there has been for several weeks, a considerable number of immig. ants at Prescott, Ontario, who are seeking tl.eir way into the United States. Buit they are objected to by the United States officers. I would not expect tli-e minister to be -able to -answer questions on that point- alt once, but I will call his attention to it so that at a future sitting he may be able to make a statement with regard to these immigrants.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will make a note of the matter and will inquire into it.

I understand the minister stated that a considerable amount of money was taken out of the estimate for the year 1904-5 to pay accounts carried over -from the year 1903-4.	1 have been
wondering if the minister was in error on that- point, for it seeps to me an extraordinary proceeding. Will the hon. minister inform me whether that is what he intended to say or not ? Was a portion of the estimate of the current year used to pay balances carried -over from the previous year, and, if so, how much ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not able at the moment to give the amount

in fact it is rather difficult (to give. It- is, I believe, a fact that there Were accounts which, had they been properly put in and certified, and had the money been available, would have been paid out of the previous year's appropriation, but which were not paid until the current year. II do not know that that is a very extraordinary condition of affairs. I am afraid that this government or possibly every government does not square up its accounts at the end of each year. In fact I have very good -reason to believe that it is not the custom of governments to be so very prompt in the payment of their accounts as to do that, and therefore, I say that there have been payments made out of the sums voted for expenditures this year to pay accounts that -properly might very well have been paid the year before.

I regret very much to hear the minister say that it is becoming ithe practice of the government to use money voted for a special purpose and apply it to another purpose. I am beginning ' to wonder whether parliament has any control over the expenditure of this country or not. It seems to me that we go through a mere form in voting estimates. We vote money for a specific purpose and then the members of the government-because the minister tells us that this is getting to he the practice of the government-turn around and use the money we vote for a specific purpose, for another purpose for which parliament never intended it. I do not know how to characterize that kind of procedure ; it is certainly highly improper ; shall I say it is dishonest ? What right has any minister to take the money which this parliament votes for any specific purpose and apply it to another purpose ? What control have we over the expenditure of this country if this kind of practice is to be continued ? I warn the Minister of the Interior that such a thing had better not occur during his regime if I am in this House because I shall enter a very strong protest and I believe the country will endorse me in every statement I make with regard to that. If there is one thing more ' than another the country will demand it is that those who are at the head of the departments, shall use the money voted by parliament for the purposes for which it is voted and that they shall not apply it to any other purpose. Is it any wonder that our expenditure is going up by leaps and bounds ? We have no control over it. We voted a large sum for immigration in 1903-4, sufficient to meet all the purposes ; we voted first a large sum in the main estimates, and then the minister came down with a supplementary estimate for sufficient to meet everything up to the end of the year. That money was cheerfully voted by parliament. Where was the necessity for taking money out of the vote for next year ? What became of the balance ? What was the authority ? What became of the money ? Was it used for some private purpose ? Was it used for some purpose unknown to this parliament ? Certainly it was used improperly if it was not available. The minister confesses it was not available. He says it wajs necessary to take money from the vote of 1904-5 in order to meet the obligations of 1903-4. If that is the case, the minister has done something else with the money, applied it to some purpose for which parliament never intended it and this procedure certainly cannot go on. What becomes of all the safeguards that we have on the treasury of this country ? We read away back in 1875 that the Prime Minister of that day lay on the treasury with a gun ; he had to sleep on it. Would to God we had a man to-day that would lie on the treasury box and protect it.

Is it not enough that
they are sleeping on the treasury benches ?
You could not find it the other night.

The hon. member says that we do not know where to find it. I am rather afraid there is a good deal of the vote which the Minister of the Interior obtained in 1903 which is some place where neither the member for Cape Breton nor myself can locate it.
I know.

The hon. member says he knows. He may have a share in it; I am not going to doubt his word, certainly he cannot give an explanation of it. The Minister of the Interior is unable to give an explanation because he told us plainly that a portion of the vote of 1904-5 had to be used to meet the expenditure of 1903-4 although that expenditure in 1903-4 was fully provided for in the main and sup-plementarv estimates. Therefore there should have been no demand made on the vote of 1904-5. I would like the Minister of the Interior to revise his statement and then when this comes before the committee again I hope that such an extraordinary condition of affairs as that which he has brought to the attention of the committtee to-night will not prevail. It is an expends ture of which I did not expect to hear, and if the Minister of the Interior never did anything more than what he has done tonight he will deserve a good deal from the people of this country for having exposed the manner in which the moneys of this country have been misappropriated in the past. I hope and trust the minister will take warning and that no such administration of the finances of this country will occur during his regime. Let me ask the minister another question. He is asking $300,000 of a supplementary estimate to meet the balance of the expenditure of the current year. I trust that is sufficient to pay everything up to the first of July. Is that the minister's intention ? That is the intention ' Now then, there should be nothing carried over, there shall be no balance carried over from 1904-u to 190o-6 because parliament when it votes the $300,000 will have voted enough to meet every expenditure in connection with immigration up to the end of the year 1904-5. How much of this $300,000 has been spent already ?

Perhaps I can relieve the minister. I am quite aware, that in the short time he has been in the department he has not had an opportunity ol tarn-

iliarizing himself -with the affairs of the department. We are prepared to make all allowances for that. May I ask if one half of this $300,000 has been spent ? Can he give an approximate estimate of the amount that has already been spent ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The position is that the money has not been spent but of course expenditure has been incurred, that is a portion of the expenditure has been incurred. It would require, as my hon. friend must be very well aware, a very close accounting, to tell just how much expenditure has been incurred up to the present time, and certainly I do not know that it is necessary for the purpose of the House and I am not prepared to give the information at the moment.

I desire to say that it is absolutely necessary we should know because if a dollar of this $300,000 has been spent it has been spent without the authority of parliament and no minister of the Crown had the right to spend one dollar in that way. If I believed to-night that the government had spent a considerable portion of that $300,000 without the consent pailiament I would stay here to a very late hour to insist that the vote be reduced by the amount that has already been expended. I have warned the Minister of the Interior in bygone years-I think the lion.
gentleman will find it on record last year_
when we were asked to recoup the government $150,000 for money that had been spent by the minister without the consent of parliament.
I made the statement then that if the same thing occurred again, I would move that the item be struck out of the estimates. Ihat is the duty of the opposition to-night. If we could ascertain how much of this $300 * 000 has been expended, how much liability has been incurred on account of it, it is our duty as a loyal opposition to stay here and to insist that the item be reduced by that amount. We must insist that the government spend no money until they have received the approbation of parliament for so doing. It is all very well for a minister to sit in his place and because he is a minister of the Crown say that he is going to use the people's money like ducks and diakes spending it here and there for any purpose that he sees fit. He has not the right to spend one dollar of it until he has come down to parliament and obtained parliament's consent. It is parliament who shall say how much we shall spend on immigration; not the minister. If parliament says we shall only expend $700,000 a year on immigration, the minister has no right to expend $701,000 nor any amount of money over the $700,000. He has no right to incur any liability beyond te amount appropriated by parliament. He must make his calculation according to the amount of money that has been voted unless he comes

down and brings in a supplementary estimate. I apprehend that the hon. gentleman is asking for a supplementary vote not only to cover what is required for completing the expenses to be incurred from the present time until the first of July, but I fear very much that he is asking ifor that very large appropriation to cover something that has been already expended, expended without the approval of parliament, expended illegally, illegitimately, and may I say, if I can use a stronger word, expended fraudulently, because it is nothing less than that. Ministers have not the right to spend money without the consent of parliament. I hope that when he comes before the committee again the hon. minister will be able to give a complete statement of this matter and I trust that there will only be a very small portion of this $300,000 already expended. If it is only a small amount we may not complain so much about it. although we have the right to complan if there is $1,000. What I desire to impress upon the hon. minister at the commencement of his career is that he must not follow the course of his predecessors. We know that it was the practice of the previous minister, year after year, to spend the peoples money without regard to the wishes of parliament. We never can control expenditure i'f ministers of the Crown are going to expend money before we vote it and without the concurrence or approval of the peoples representatives and I am quite sure that the hon. Minister of the Interior at the inception of his career will desire to do his work as faithfully and as honestly as possible and that he desires to stand in good faith with the House. In order to do that I must insist that he will not presume to expend $1,000 on account of immigration or of any other branch of his department until the concurrence of parliament has been received.

I think the hon. Minister of the Interior is deserving of very great credit for the exposure he has made of the practices of the government in the past. I do not know whether the slap he took at the old ministers was mended or not, but I think it has given to the committee a good insight into the conduct of these hon. gentlemen. I believe it is now up to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) the leader of the House at the present time, to give some explanation of the conduct of the government in allowing these over expenditures to go on in the various departments of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I wiish to give all the information that can be given to hon. gentlemen opposite and I certainly wish to have their good-will in the performance of such duties as have been laid upon me. I think that perhaps the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) has been scarcely fair in the construction he has placed upon what

I have said. I would not say at all that he was inaccurate, but, as a matter of fact, any danger that he might apprehend of fraud or trespassing upon the public right in the matter of taking money that has no been voted is, I take it for granted, very efficiently guarded against by that watchdog of the treasury, the Auditor General. There is no danger of money being taken except under an appropriation as long as that gentleman remains in office and I presume as long as any successor, if he is charged with the same duty and placed in the same control, remains in office.

Suppose the liability is incurred before it comes before the Auditor General and then suppose parliament should refuse to ratify any unwarranted action of the minister, where would the Auditor General he and where would the minister be ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The amounts which were incurred in the previous year and which the government honestly owed were placed in the estimates for the current- year. They were not paid without 'being placed in the estimates. They have been placed in the estimates for the current year and are paid in due and legal course after parliament has voted the money. I mentioned the question of the tents supplied to the Barr colony as one of these cases. This was an account incurred two years ago and it is only being paid this year, but it is being paid, not outside of the authority of parliament, but with the authority of parliament and in due and legal form. Such is the case in regard to all these items.
HUGHE'S. Why was the $18,000, which is only being paid this year for these tents, not paid last year ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Or by Governor General's warrants.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Or by Governor General's warrants. The facts in regard to immigration are as I stated in the remarks I made in presenting the vote. When we undertake the work of inducing people to come to this country and to settle if our efforts are successful beyond the means we have provided we must either render that expenditure we have already made useless, or not provide at a critical time for immigration that has come, or we must provide for that immigration when it does come. There is no person who wishes well to the cause of immigration in this country who would say that in the case of these Bari- colonists they should have been le'ft to shiver and die on the prairie in the spring snow storms for the lack of tents until parliament had been asked to vote the money for these tents.
Was not parliament in session ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Our experience is that it sometimes takes a good while to get a vote from parliament, and a woman or child will freeze to death in one night. I do not think we could afford to take chances in such a case. So long as I occupy the position I do, I will have no hesitation in asking the House to condone the offience, if it is an offence, of providing for the urgent needs of immigrants if they should come here in numbers beyond the provision we have made for them. This is more than a question of dollars and cents ; it is a matter of life and death ; it will not wait. We cannot afford to wait, and I have no doubt that both the House and the country will sustain the minister who takes immediate action under such circumstances.

The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) used very strong language with regard to over-expenditure, but his language is

quite as applicable to tlie former Conservative government as to this government. As far back as 1892-3 the sum appropriated by parliament was not sufficient to meet the expenditure for several fiscal years. In that year and the two succeeding fiscal years the sum of $150,000 was voted. In 1892-3 the appropriation of $150,000 was. however, not sufficient to pay all the liabilities Incurred in that year, and the sum of $31,401.09 was carried forward and paid out of the next year's vote. During the fiscal year 1893-4 the sum of $149,998.80 was expended, practically wiping out the appropriation of $150,000, but there was not sufficient to pay all the liabilities contracted in that year, and it was necessary to carry over $81,874.20 to the following fiscal year; that sum was paid out of the vote of 1894-5. During 1894-5 the whole of the appropriation of $150,000 was expended, with the exception of a few. dollars, such expenditure including the $81,874.20 which was contracted in the previous year and had to be paid out of the vote for 1894-5. About this time the immigration business had practically ceased, and for the year 1895-0 only $84,915 was voted for general immigration expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
test.	Who has the right to say to
what extent the immigration policy of this country will he pursued ? Is it the minister of his own will ? What kind of a king is lie ? No minister has the right to set up his own individual opinion against the opinion of 214 men in the House of Commons. Surely the minister will concede that he was in error when he made his statement, and that in future he must in every case limit himself to the amount voted by parliament.
I trust that the minister will remember, when he comes to deal with immigration during the coming year, exactly how much money parliament has authorized him to expend for that purpose, and will carry on the service in accordance with that amount ; and that if he thinks he could bring in another 50,000 immigrants by means of the expenditure of $300,000 more, he will not expend that without the consent of parliament. No minister would be justified in pursuing any such policy. Pariiament has a right to control the government's immigration policy, and does control it by the amount of money it votes for that purpose. I want the minister for the coming year simply to cut his garment in accordance with'the amount of cloth this parliament provides him with-not to expend $1,000 more on immigration than parliament says ought to be spent-until such time, at any rate, as he comes down to parliament again and asks for a supplementary vote, not after he lias spent the money, but before fie has spent it. There is no doubt that this is the true constitutional spirit of spending public money. If ministers are going to spend money right and left, according to their own will, what is the use of parliament ? We might as well adopt the estimates as a whole and say nothing about them ; we might as well vote them in a lump sum. and go home, if that is-all the control parliament is going to have over the expenditure. I trust that the minister will start out in the coming year with a correct idea of what his duty and privileges are in this respect, and will not go back two years or five years to copy what some previous Minister of the Interior has done, and expect that the action of any previous minister will be accepted as a justification for him. I think we would not discharge our duty on this side of the House were we to permit a procedure of that kind to go on year after year without raising our voices against it. But I apprehend that after the expiration of another year we shall not be called on to speak so forcibly on this matter, because I believe the minister will realize what his duty is, and will give effect to that.
