There is one phase of this question upon which I desire some information from the hon. Minister of the Interior. I would like to know whether at the present time any efforts are being made, either by advertisement, literature or otherwise, to induce immigrants to come from the southern portions of Europe to this country ? We all feel that we cannot have too many immigrants of a desirable class, and yet that it is very easy for us to have too many of an undesirable class. I quote from the * Daily Telegraph ' of Quebec of Friday the following :
is no intention to encourage the coming of people from the continent of Europe who are not agriculturists as well as desirable from a physical point of view. The fact that stringent medical examinations are made and that so many are deported, who are found to be suffering from disease, is evidence of the intention of the department. I presume that the reason there have been so many cases of diseased immigrants during recent months is that probably the same attention was not paid in past years, but when it is thoroughly known that this strict supervision is exercised we will have fewer instances of diseased people coming to the country.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The same complaint has been made the last two or three years ?

Are these shipped back and dumped in Scotland ?
The Donaldson liner steamship ' Athenian1 arrived in port yesterday afternoon from Glasgow. She had on board fifty foreigners who will be deported- on instructions from the government officials. On arrival at Quebec the vessel was inspected, and it was found that a large number of the steerage passengers were afflicted with trachoma. A number of those slightly attacked were taken to the house of detention at Quebec for treatment, while the remainder came on to Montreal. Dr. Laberge, city health officer, and a number of his men met the boat on its arrival, and after his inspection he refused to allow any of the affected ones to come ashore.
This is only one instance. We are constantly receiving a class of immigrants who are affected with loathsome diseases, and we wish to know whether any of the money of the Dominion is being expended to attract this undesirable class ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The department is not expending any money and keeps no agencies in any part of the continent of Europe except in France and Belgium'. There are two or three agents in France and one in Belgium. They have, however, an arrangement with a steamship organization which operates, not from a southern port, but from Hamburg.

While admitting the desirability of securing agricultural immigrants,
I do not think the fact that a man is an agriculturist is necessarily proof that he .is desirable. It seems to me that the experience of the department should have shown it that there are some sections Irom which it is not desirable to bring immigrants, and the Hamburg company should he prevented from exploiting those portions of the continent. WThen people are found to be suffering from a loathsome disease, which is proof that they are of filthy habits, the department should notify the steamship company that we do not wish any efforts made to recruit grants from certain parts of Europe. Experience shows plainly where these people come from, and the steamship companies should be warned not to recruit people from those sections.

The hon. minister says that the immigrants from the continent are to be taken from the farms, does that apply to the British Islands also ? Because a number of our best farmers in the Northwest to-day were not brought up in the rural districts. I know of one who came out from London and who never saw the green country until he left England. He was a pastry cook at home and ne is now one of the best farmers m Manitoba. One of the best farmers m the Prince Albert district used to be a watch-maker m Paris. Another was a clerk m a shop in Paris. The trouble with these continental farmers is that they have to unlearn a lot and you have to instill into them the Northwest system of farming. What you want is men of energy, with a clean heart and person and free from disease, and I care not whether men of that kind come from

the city or the country, they will make a success.

We are getting a large portion of our immigration from some countries of Europe which do not furnish us with desirable settlers. iCan it be possible that the government have no supervision over immigrants before they leave their native country ? There is a general impression where I live that we have not been getting the right class of immigrants into the Northwest. A large percentage of the immigration is not of a desirable class, and our people would rather do without settlers than have settlements of that kind. Such people cost the country a lot of money not only to bring them here, but to assist them from time to time after they get here

Re Delivery of Scrip.
It has always been an invariable rule of the department to refuse to recognize assignments or powers of attorney as authority for the delivery of half-breed land scrip, and the regulations already referred to of the 6th June, 1901, specifically provided ' that in cases in which a half-breed asks for land scrip, the commissioner has no authority to accept or act upon any assignment or power of attorney.'
It has also been the practice where the scrip certificate was not delivered to the claimant personally by the commissioner, to send his scrip by registered mail to his own address in care of any person designated therein, upon a written request being filed in the department over the claimant's own signature, attested by two witnesses, who must certify as to the identification of the claim, and one of the witnesses must also make an affidavit as to the execution of such order. The scrip, which was issued in satisfaction of the claims referred to, was forwarded on orders which were prepared in the manner above indicated.
Re Location of the Scrip Issued under the Order in Council of 13th August, 1904.
By departmental letter of the 10th March last, addressed to all agents of Dominion lands, the agents were advised that it had been decided to allow scrip, granted the half-breed residents of the United States under the said Order in Council of the 13th August, 1904, to be located in the name of the grantee thereof by the holder of such scrip without requiring the grantee to appear personally at the land agency to make his entry. It was also pointed out that the applicant for location should make the application over his own signature on behalf of the person named on the scrip note, and in all respects comply with the rules and regulations governing the location of half-breed land scrip, and that, as heretofore, assignments of these locations executetd by the half-breeds prior to the date on which the land was entered for in the manner above indicated, would not be recognized by the department.

There has been a good deal of talk about these homestead inspectors in. the last few years. Since my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) has taken charge of the department we expect a good many reforms, and I am sure we shall not be disappointed. May I ask what policy the department has with regard to the homestead inspectors-whether they are to be permitted to become active politicians or not ?

It is certainly not the policy to have them acting as active politicians, except as we hope that the satisfaction they will give the public in their work will be to the political credit of the government in power.

I am sure the minister (Mr. Oliver) knows the purport of the question.
It has been stated, and I do not know that it has ever been denied that in the election that took place the officers of the Interior Department to a greater or less extent were made or made themselves active political workers in the campaign. I should feel like this with reference to this vote-that if the minister proposes to follow the same course that has been followed, and that in asking for the vote for new inspectors he should be asking a vote for men part of whose time is to be taken up in political work, it will take a long time for the item to pass. I do not think it is right or honest, and I do not think it is good politics in the long run.
I hope my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver), from whom we expect a good deal, in this way at least, will be able to say to the committee that homestead inspectors and other officers for whom we vote money shall not be allow-6u to become active workers in political campaigns, that they shall be homestead inspectors, or whatever officials they are, and

that they shall attend to the work assigned to them and attend to it solely. That, of course, we all admit to be the right plan and I think it is the plan which we might agree to have carried out. I would like to hear what the hon. minister's views are on that question.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would not like, in consequence of any stand I would take or any admission I would make, to be thought to admit that it has been any part of the policy of the department to have their homestead inspectors act as political agents. I can assure the committee that as far as my say goes, I quite agree with my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster). To put it on the lowest ground I do not consider it good politics to have homestead inspectors or other government officials acting as active government agents. I think they can do their party as well as the country very much better service by attending to their duties and performing them in an efficient manner. I think that would reflect the most credit on the government and on the party.

In reference to what the hon. minister has said I have a copy of the Regina ' Daily Standard ' of the 14th April, at the time he was going up to contest the seat in Edmonton. There is an item in the issue of that date which says :
Walter Scott, M.P., for this constituency, went west this morning to assist in the fight at Edmonton. He was accompanied by P. Talbot, M.P., J. G. Turriff, M.P., P. M. Bredt, assistant commissioner of immigration, and S. P. Porter, homestead inspector.
I do not know whether it is really the case that these gentlemen went up. I believe that Mr. Bredt and Mr. Porter are both exceedingly active politicians and that they were especially so during the last election. We have had some experience of them in the past if this statement is not true in this particular case.

speechtext:
Is this gentleman a Doukhobor?
Mr, LAKE. Schukin is a Doukhobor. He with several others was persuaded by the late Mr. Crearer to make a homestead entry. Of course, it was very much in the interest of these people and the Northwest generally that they should make entries and own their own lands.. Schukin and about thirty others made their entries and cut themselves loose from the community system. When Mr. Verigin came he apparently insisted upon the establishment of the community system with the result that this became a regular part of their organization and pressure is being put upon a few Doukhobors who were beginning to make individual entries for land to force'them back into the community system.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not able just at this time to declare any distinct policy in regard to the administration of that particular part of the department, but I will say that I would not think it part of the duty of the government or of the department to assist in any way in enforcing the peculiar beliefs in regard to religion or social life that may be held by the Doukhobors or any other people. In regard to the ease mentioned, I have no knowledge of it other than what is stated by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) but it would seem to me that whilst the person mentioned has possibly suffered a hardship it would be no less a hardship to give to him the patent for the land upon which a whole village was situated. It would seem to me from the statement of the case to be one in which there must be a hardship either to one individual or to a large number and that the department had decided that the hardship should be suffered by the one rather than the large number.	.

I have a report here amongst the other papers. I did not know this opening would present itself at this moment to take the subject up and I did not get it very well prepared, but I would like to read 204

a report from the homestead inspector of the Yorkton district in regard to this case. Perhaps it would show the hon. minister clearly what one of his officials thinks about the matter. After reporting on the land fin the ordinary form and as to the value of the improvements which had been made he adds this further report :
I further report and say to my knowledge that in the fall of 1902, Mr. James Crearer, deceased, who was then immigration agent at this point, was anxious that the Doukhobors should make entries for their lands, visited" these people and tried to induce them to make-entries and the people did not respond as they appeared to be undecided as to what course to pursue. The community system did not then exist among them and everything went along all right and the others made no objection until Mr. Peter Verigin arrived in their midst and started the community system.
Mr. Schukin would not join the community so they asked him to get off the place and made it very disagreeable for him ever since and would not allow him to cultivate his homestead. I consider that it would be a hardship to turn him off as all the lands for a long distance are now entered and he would have to go a long way from his friends in order to get a homestead.
And further, the statement made by Simeon Reifen is not correct regarding the mill which he claims is on this land. It is on the S W \ of this section.
About half of the houses now on this land were built since Mr. Schukin obtained his entry although aware of his entry.
I understand also that ten out of the sixteen families are leaving said village in the spring to be located in other villages near their homesteads. Six families will remain for some time until their present buildings become use- . less which will only be a short time and they will not be disturbed by Mr. Schukin. There is another letter from a gentleman who resides in that district, a gentleman who I think has always been a staunch supporter of the Liberal party and he takes very strong ground with reference to the Doukhobor question and as to the manner in which Mr. Peter Verigin is acting. It may be as well to have this letter placed on ' Hansard,' as I think the whole [DOT]subject should be discussed and laid before the House. This gentleman writes :
Devil's Lake, Dec. 16, 1904. Commissioner of Dominion Lands,
Dear Sir,-I take the liberty of writing you a few lines regarding the Doukhobors here. There are about thirty here that have left the company. They have got out and are working on their homesteads. They have become British subjects and are falling in line with the laws of the country.

And then we have Mr. Peter Verigin with his company. Just now they are cutting and hauling spruce Jogs. I don't think there will he a standing tree of any account within miles of here after this winter. They will not register births, marriages or deaths, nor yet will they become British subjects, and Peter will tell you he would like to become a British subject himself but his people would not hear of it. He is working hard to keep the company together. He tells them if they leave the company, they leave the land, for he says he owns all the land round here and they will have to move one -hundred miles from here. So these men that Slave left the company are in doubt if they will get an entry for their land or not. I tell them they will get it and I hope you will be of the same opinion. Now, these Doukhobors that have left the company tell me that Peter Verigin was the cause of them not taking up their land when they came here. He kept writing to them not to take up land until he would get here, and when he gets here he tells them to keep to work and he would go to Yorkton and take up the land for them.
I may mention that this correspondence appears to show that a great number of entries for lands upon which these villages were situated have been cancelled and that the new entries for the men who have been deprived of the old entries have been taken up by Mr. Peter Verigin.
Of course he gets the credit of them taking up their land. One can see by the actions of those that have left the company and have fallen in line with the laws of the country that Peter Verigin is the cause of the company men not falling in line with the laws of the country. I am told that he went into the land office at Yorkton and told them that he had eighteen men dissatisfied with their homesteads and would like to change it for another. Now, this homestead that he would like to change, were homesteads of these men that had left the company, and they knew nothing of Peter Verigin trying to cancel their homesteads at that time, but they found out in time and went to Yorkton to the land office and told them that they were quite satisfied with their homesteads. There was another man here, he (Peter Verigin) went to the land office and reported that he -syas dead and had his place cancelled and one of his company men put on it. I know for a fact the man who Peter Verigin reported dead is going around here feeling bad about losing his place. There is another man here by the name of Eone Sugan on the northeast quarter of section 33, T. 31, R. 6, W. 2. Peter Verigin is trying hard to cancel his place.
The Eone Sugan referred to here is the man whose case I am calling attention to :
This £ugan says that he heard that Peter Verigin had written to you about it. This Eone Sugan was among the first of the Doukhobors to enter for his land. There was no company when Sugan entered for his land. Peter Verigin had not come at that time. The late Mr. Crearer, the immigration agent, was out here to see if he could get them to enter for their land, and they had a letter from Verigin at that time to not enter for their land until he got here. I was along with Mr. Crearer at the time he made an offer to any Doukhobor that would enter for his homestead the choice of anv quarter at Devil lake, so Sugan said he would

take the quarter he was living on. He paid his ten dollars, got his entry, has done his homestead duties. He has become a British subject. I think a man like this should not be cast to one side and a man like Verigin get the preference. Peter Verigin and his interpreter have gone into the land office and reported false statements to them. He said the grist mill was on Eone Sugan's quarter. I took the surveyor's chain and measured from the nearest point from the line to the mill. It was 3 chains, 274 links from Eone Sugan's quarter. Peter Verigin, at the land office, said that they had quite a bit of ploughing done on it. Sugan was ploughing on his farm when a number came down to him with their teams and ploughed. They gave him ten minutes to get out of the field. He unhitched his horses and took them to the stable, and they pitched his plough into the fence. Please do the best you can for him.
Yours truly,

This letter is dated the 10th of Decmber, 1904. It will, I think, be found from other papers in the department that unfortunately this man's entry had already been cancelled. He had left the rest of the Doukoho-bors to take up land and to become a good British subject and fulfil the duties of citizenship. But apparently on the word of Mr. Peter Verigin he was deprived of his property and sent off to start life anew on another homestead. The case appears to me to be a particularly bad one. A man who becomes a British subject and tries to be a good citizen, even though a Doukhobor should be protected just the same as any other British subject.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not see that it would be possible to make compensation, and I would not like to judge the case until I have heard both sides. A very grave accusation is made against this man Peter Verigin and of course we will have to hear his side before giving a decision. I would not like to make any statement now as to what will be done in the matter. It has been suggested to me that it is entirely improbable that this man's entry was made before the village was established on the lands. As every one knows, when the Doukhobors come into any section of the country the

first thing they do is to form into a village on the land so that on the face of it the probability would be that the village was on the land before this man made his entry. However, if he had an entry first I would certainly think he was entitled to it. No doubt the deparmtent took action believing it was the lesser of two evils ; an injustice to be done either to the one family or to fifteen or twenty families, and they decided perhaps to let the one man suffer.

In reference to the question as to whether the village is on the land or not the report of Mr. McCallum says :
About half of the village houses now on this 'land were built since Schukin claimed his entry, although aware of the entry.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What about the other halt ?

I presume, although there is nothing to show it, that Mr. Schukin went on to the land with the other Douk-hobors and they built the village together.
That, after all, is not the point. After he and others had been established in the village, Mr. Orearer, the immigration agent, now dead, who to those people represented the power of the government, came down and asked them to make entries for their land, and according to both of these reports offered them any section they chose to enter for ; and he gave Mr. Schukin the entry for the land he occupied. I do not think the government should go back on that entry. Mr. Schukin made the entry in good faith, and since that time he has apparently resided there and performed his cultivation duties ; and if he is not allowed to retain the land it will be a great breach of faith on the part of the government, and will be likely to prevent these people leaving the community system.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of course, I would not like to speak of the conduct of the agent, who is now dead ; but I would call the attention of the committee to the fact that however wrong he may have been, the homesteader was certainly in the wrong in entering for the homestead, when he knew that other people were in occupation of it and had made improvements upon it, which my hon. friend knows is entirely contrary to the letter and the spirit of the Homestead Act. He entered for the homestead with the knowledge that there were other families occupying the land, whose prior rights in it were just as good as his; and although he held the homestead entry, he permitted still other people to come on that same land and build on it and occupy it. I do not think he can hold himsel'f to be altogether the aggrieved party in the transaction. He did commit a wrong with his eyes open. He may have acted under misinformation in entering for land that was already in the occupation of other people, and he was not protecting his own interest as he ought to have done when he 204*
permitted still other people to go on and occupy and make improvements on that land.

The hon. minister must remember that the Doukhobors were not at that time very well acquainted with our laws and customs. They were brought out in a way as wards of the government. They were put upon their land under the direction of the government officials. When the chief government official in that quarter comes to one of them and says :	You
can have the entry of this land, I want you people to make entries for your land ; and this man says, if you give me the entry for the land I am living on, I will make it, I do not think he did with his eyes open what he knew to be a wrong. He was told that he was at liberty to make that entry by Mr. Orearer, who at that time held a very good position under the department.

I do not think the Doukhobors can make the plea that my hon. friend makes, that they did not understand the laws of the country, because, if there was one thing that was explained to them time after time, it was the homestead laws and the homestead conditions. I think 1 am right when I say that all these Doukhobof villages were established before any homestead entries were made. This very difficulty was 'foreseen, and it was suggested to the people that in making entries it would not be advisable for them to enter for the quarter sections on which the village was to be located. This man evidently had been living there for probably two or three years before he made a homestead entry at all. He knew perfectly well that this village was on this land, and I do not see how lie could make the entry knowing that, because he would have to make an affidavit that there were no improvements and no people living on the land. X think the better plan if it could be managed would be for the department to allow the homesteader to retain his homestead, but to allow him the privilege of disposing of five or ten acres that may be occupied as a village, and sell it to the community. The difficulty has arisen largely in this way. At the time this homesteader made the entry, I do not suppose he had any intention of acting on his own account. These villages are ail separate business communities, having no business connection with each other, the people in each village owning everything in common, and I presume that his idea in making entry for the homestead, was that it would become common property in the future ; but he has apparently changed his mind. I may say that the department did everything in their power to induce these people to make their entries at the proper time, foreseeing that there would be difficulty from delay. They did delay for a long

time, and there will be some little difficulty, but I think it is a matter that can be easily got over by the department.

I hope this matter will not be lost sight o>f by the Department of the Interior. I notice a telegram here signed J. W. Greenway, Department of the Interior, to Peter Verigin, Esq., and dated the 12th of December, 1904 :
Entry Ivan Schukin Northwest twenty-three, thirty-one, six west second, cancelled, being Doukhobors village site.
That means that the entry has been cancelled. I also notice another telegram here, dated Yorkton, December 13 :
Verigin acting lor Doukhobors here Saturday and yesterday. All re-entries of Doukhobors completed ; forty-three entries granted them.
The reason I call attention to this second telegram is that it seems to me undesirable that one man should make a bunch of entries in that way for these communities, especially holding the position which he appears to do in the Doukhobor community. It tends to keep in their minds the idea that the lands are being entered by the community as a body, and not for the individual.

The question, I think, the minister will admit, is a rather serious one. It is not simply the case of this one Doukhobor, but it seems to go further than that. The peculiar system that the Doukhobors have may be the best, looked at from their point of view, and there may be, in the earlier days of settlement, some good features in it, in the way of massing together for support and bringing large numbers together, which would recommend it to a certain extent in the eyes of Canadians who are not in favour of that system, of course. But X think we ought to keep this in view ; that if there be any person who wishes to assert his individuality and become a British subject and conform to all our laws, and work on the same line as individual holders, he ought to be very carefully supported by the department, at least to this extent, that the leader of such a settlement, who naturally has great powers, .and naturally also, I suppose, wants to keep those intact and make them greater if he can, does not become in a way arbitrary and to a certain extent tyrannical, and by the great influence he has, keep down and utterly make impossible this assertion of individuality.
I think that the department ought at least to see that such influence is not exercised m an arbitrary and tyrannical manner so as to prevent any individual getting his land. Of course it is easy to say that if one is pitted against the many, the one must suffer and not the many. But you can turn that right around and sav that a good many are better able to make up Mr. TURRIFF.
the loss to the one than he is to bear it alone. If this man made his entry in good faith and then is driven out, the department should seek some way of making the matter even for him, but I do not know that the department should suffer. Probably if the fault were entirely with the officers of the department, that would be a fair way to consider it ; but if the interests of the one must be sacrificed to the interests of the many, then the many ought to make compensation. I am not sure that some arrangement such as has been suggested might not be made, namely, to allow the person who entered in good faith to keep his homestead and dispose of whatever portion of it is necessary for the village. The village is not going to run over the' whole ICO acres. In that way the village would get what it wants and the man who holds the property around the village would have its value enhanced. But what I would like to emphasize is this, that the department should look into this matter and see that a remedy is at once applied, if necessary.

It is not merely one case apparently, but 43 cases. I do not know whether there were 43 villages founded previously to these lands being entered for, but I have here a letter which I had better read :
Otradnoe Village, October 18, 1904.
John Obed Smith,
Commissioner of Immigration,
Winnipeg, Manitoba.
Dear Sir,-We have just finished in finding out the homesteads which are under Doukhobors villages, and have found correctly. The list of villages and proper homesteads which are under villages we beg to inclose you herewith, kindly look into this matter, and leave those homesteads for villages, making them free from homestead entries. If any homestead entry was made for land, which is under villages, so that was made by mistake, as I told you. In every village there is one free homestead, which was given for village in wrong place, and which can be changed now for man whose land is under village.
Yours faithfully,

Then follows a list of some 43 different villages. Apparently Verigin had gone in to Yorkton and changed those entries for 43 other entiles. It is quite possible there may be great hardship on other men whose lands have been taken away from them with the improvements thereon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know that I can add to what has been said. It is no part of the business of the department to assist the peculiar religious ideas of any people whoever they may be. Our business is with the individual settler and to protect his rights. A very grave statement has been made which will have to be investigated and action taken. With regard to the individual case mentioned, this man

641S
does not come to us with, clean hands, and therefore has not that claim for consideration which he would have if he came with an absolutely clear case. The good faith of the agent who had to deal with this man is called in question. That agent is now dead and we are compelled to take the evidence of other men as to what he said and did ; and I do not know that we would be quite justified in accepting in full everything that many be said regarding this deceased officer.
There may be records and letters. '

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We must judge of the case as we find it, aside from the question as to what he is reported to have said or done.

This Doukhobor, matter has been before the House several times. It was a mistake bringing them into the country at all, and that was the view taken by the minister himself. They are living in communities, and I should like to know how many of them have homesteads and whether they have made any provision to repay the money they borrowed from the government. I should like to know whether the assurance given us by Mr. Smart, ex-deputy minister, that this debt would be held against the land is correct. This statement was made before they took out any homesteads, and I do not see how dt could be entered against the land when they had no claim on it. How much has been paid on the debt and is there any lien on the land homestead for that indebtedness ? It will be pretty hard to divide up the indebtedness and register it against the property of each individual. Some arrangement should be made by the leaders of the Doukhobors to pay back the money lent. I understand they are a rather prosperous community although they do not fall into our ways. My hon. friend the minister (Mr. Oliver) made the statement In former days that the country would be better off without them. I quite agreed with him then, and have not seen any great reason for changing my mind since.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. U. Wilson) to say that he desires certain information. His request will be attended to ; and if it is the pleasure of the committee to pass the item as it stands in the supplementary estimates, I will guarantee to have an answer toy the time we reach the main estimates.

The only trouble is that so many of these questions are postponed that some of them are sure to be forgotten. The hon. minister has his officer beside him, and I think he might give us at least some of the information we require at once. These questions, it seems to me, might easily have been anticipated. The official must toe familiar with the facts, I
should think. They have been before the Agriculture Committee time and again, and have been threshed out fully in this House.
IMr, TURRIFF. I may state that there were about 8,000 of these Doukhobors, men, women and children.
How much have they increased ?

I do not know. That is a matter that the local government attends to. A year ago these people had practically all made homestead entries-between 1,800 and 2.000. I think. There are about thirty-five of the Doukhobors, as I understand, who have, as it were, broken away from the communal system and taken out naturalization papers. I agree with every word that has been said by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), that those individuals who wish to break away from the communal system should be given every possible consideration by the department. I wish to say, however^ that while they have been troublesome in connection with their homestead entries, the Doukhobors have been a good class of settlers. And they are doing well. I do not know whether they have been paying back what money they owed or not ; * but they are in a position to pay back or will toe very shortly, because they have prospered wonderfully well. They are very industrious, and no doubt the work they have done under Peter Verigin has been good work. I think there is no doubt that his influence so far has been good materially-that he has been a good business head, and under him the people there have progressed very well. Still, I do not think that it is in the interest of this coun-trv that anv one man should be the practical dictator over 7.000 or 8,000 people. Therefore, any encouragement that can be given to individuals to break away from the communal system, I think, should be given.

Perhaps the hon. member for East Assiniboia (Mr. Tuniftl can tell us whether they follow the communal system so far as their earnings are concerned. Do their earnings go into one fund, or are they living like other people ?

With the exception of the thirty-five to which I have referred, I think they are all living in the communal system, that is to say, each village is a business community by itself. It has no business connection with the other villages, but in each village everything is owned in common.
Mr. LAKE'. Referring to what the hon. member for East Assiniboia (Mi. luniff) has said about the local government keeping the record of the increase, I think I ought to say that the local government have had considerable difficulty in carrying on that work. That recalls to my memory a matter which was brought to my notice some time

back which I would like the minister to inquire into when he is looking up the other things in regard to this settlement. Some time last year a Doukhobor was found hanged in a stable. I would like to know whether that fact was ever called to the attention of the authorities, whether it was reported by Mr. Verigin, and whether any inquest was held.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is no part of the business of this department to take notice of anything of that nature. However, I will make inquiries if it is thought desirable.
I would like the minister to tell us whether Mr. Smart, the ex-deputy minister, is now connected with the department ; and, if so, what is his position ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Smart is not now employed by the department.

It is not long since he was employed by the department as special agent in the west. I do not know what his duties were, but I believe he was paid $10 a day and expenses. Can the minister tell us how long it is since Mr. Smart was employed by the department ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Since Mr. Smart resigned his position as deputy minister he has not been in the employ of the government except in special service. He was employed a month or two ago in conducting a delegate of the Austrian government through the Northwest. He also made a visit to the United States, looking into the quarantine arrangements there.
side the offices, but outside the vote for civil government.

I notice that in the charges for Dominion lands the salaries for clerks amount to $31,101.27. Do I understand that that includes all the clerks in the Interior Department, or only those connected with Dominion lands ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Only those in the Dominion lands branch.
How many officers are employed in this branch ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This item is for service altogether out of Ottawa, and I am not prepared to answer that question.
It distinctly says clerks at Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The salaries which are provided under civil government are for what is called the inside service, and everything that is not under that head is called the outside service, whether the persons are employed in Ottawa or at outside offices. This increase of $10,000 for salaries for the outside service, is for the purpose of meeting the requirements in the outside agencies chiefly, owing to the increase of business there ; arid this increase of business does not occur simply because of an increase of settlement, but because the settlers of some years ago are now in a position to draw their patents, and that causes a great increase of clerical work in the different land offices.
Rut he is not now employed by the department ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not in any capacity.
When engaged in connection with quarantine, .he was paid, I suppose, by the Department of Agriculture ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. Mr. Smart was not engaged in superintending quarantine, but was looking into the operation as affecting the immigration. Of course, the immigrants are the ones to get the benefit of the quarantine, and Mr. Smart was looking into the regulations from the immigrant's point of view.

As I understand i the $12,000 additional and the $10,000 add tional are largely for clerks, in the origin; estimate the minister asked $12,357 of a increase, and that apparently is for exti clerks in the department. Do I understan that all these sums are practically for exti assistance ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The sum of $12,000 required for contingencies includes all salaries for homestead inspectors and officers who work outside. Then the amount of $10,000 is for salaries for increases in the staff in offices throughout the west. The item here says outside service,' but that means, not out-Mr. LAKE.

On page L-91 of the Auditor General's Report I notice ' Dominion Lands, salaries of extra clerks at head office, and advertising.' Then it says ' Salaries Of clerks at Ottawa, $31,110.27.' Now, I understand that these votes of $12,000 and $10,000 the minister is asking for are to pay further extra clerks. In that view I would like an explanation of that statement on page L-91.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The figures I have here show total increases in salaries amounting to $19,239, and decreases caused by resignations, transfers, &c., amount to $9,229, leaving a net increase of $10,010. This covers the extras here in the Ottawa office, and the extra service required in the land offices in the Territories.

I realize that I cannot expect the hon. minister to be thoroughly conversant with all the figures. But I would like his deputies to explain wThy this appears in the Auditor General's Report in the manner it does.
'Mr. OLIVER, There are a number of clerks listed as extra clerks, but that does not mean that they are employed as extras for work in this particular year. They are clerks who have been employed for a greater or lesser time, but they are not on the

permanent list, and therefore they are called extras. These are in what is called the inside service, and are not connected with this vote of ,$10,000 we are asking for.
They are practically permanent, inasmuch as you have kept them every year.
What was the amount in the main vote ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Salaries for outside service amount to $137,900.
On what page of the estimates is that ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That sum of $137,900 does not appear in the estimates of this year, but in last year's estimates, on page 71, m the column of 1904-5.
The minister spoke of Mr. Smart's work in accompanying the Austrian delegate.' What does that mean ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not personally familiar with the object of the delegate in visiting Ottawa, as that took place before I assumed office. But. I am given to understand that he was the commissioner of the Austrian government, who were desirous of having exact information as to how the colonists from that country were progressing on the continent of America. This commissioner was sent out to investigate the Austrian colonies in the United States and Canada. It was thought desirable, I presume, to treat him with the greatest courtesy and to facilitate his movements and his getting the fullest information to the greatest possible degree. Therefore, the department took every means to facilitate his tour through Canada, and as Mr. Smart had been in charge of the Interior Department and of the immigration branch as well, and was familiar with the work, it was thought desirable that he should have the conduct of the delegate through Canada
Is the hon. minister pre pared to say just why Mr. Smart left his office as deputy ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no knowledge of the subject.

It seems rather odd that we have had no sufficient explanation of it. Mr Smart is supposed to have been and is generally acknowledged to have been an efficient deputy. He seems to have taken a great deal of interest in his department, and as far as the testimony from the government side of the House was concerned he was fulfilling his duties well. All at once and very suddenly he seems to have departed that office and the only explanation we got in the House from the minister was that he left it because he had a chance of bettering his financial position. Quite a long while has passed since then and Mr. Smart seems
still to be here, and the fact that he is taking these special services up for the government would rather militate against that. I thought the hon. minister probably might know and be able to give us the explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no knowledge of the matter whatever. The resignation was handed in before the session of parliament occurred and there has nothing come to my knowledge in regard to it. I presume that any officer of the government is at liberty to leave if he sees fit without giving any reason and I presume that is what occurred in this case.
The hon. minister is asking for an increase of $20,000 in the mines branch of his department. May I ask what they intend doing in that branch during the coming year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not an increase ; it is a transfer from the civil government vote to the Dominion Lands vote. It is merely a transfer from one vote to another within the department.
At page 71 of the estimates, under the column of increases, is placed this $20,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course it is an increase in the lands branch, but if my hon. friend will turn to civil government he will see that it shows as a decrease. At page 13, it shows in the estimate for civil government as a decrease just as on page 71 under the heading of Dominion lands it shows as an increase.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. minister stated that Mr. Smart was not in the employ of the government now in any position. How long is it since he ceased to be in the employ of the government ?

I cannot give the date off hand, but Mr. Smart has not been in the employ of the government since he returned from the west in company with the Austrian delegate, which would be in the latter days of April.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I think, if my hon. friend will look at 1 Hansard ' of only a short time ago he will find a question which I put to the ' government the answer to which indicated that he was then in the employ of the government and receiving $10 a day. It is only a short time ago since that question was answered by some acting minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It probably was an error if the question was later than the 1st ot May.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I suppose a portion of this $10 000 is to make up extras to him since he has left the department as deputy minister ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Smart's expenses in that connection would have no connection with this vote at all. They would come in

connection with immigration. This was distinctly a matter of immigration work.
Further amount required for maintenance, construction of roads and bridges, and other necessary works in connection with the Hot Springs Reservation, near Banff, Northwest Territories, $7,000.

speechtext:

What are the salaries of the officials for the year ? It would seem as if only eight months salaries were voted unless you have made large additions to the staff which I hope has not been done. Ml'- OLIVER. The salaries, as I understand the information given to me here have not been increased nor has the number of officers.

speechtext: No.
What is the necessity for printing 30.000 pamphlets on Banff.

speechtext: On tender ?

speechtext: I am not able to answer but I rather think it was not, because it is a very fine class of work and could not very well be let by tender.

What is the system of distribution ? I should think that it should be distributed amongst the great outside world to announce that we have natural beauties here and are making and maintaining parks. The method of distribution would be very important in the case of a pamplet of this kind.

speechtext: We sent a copy to each senator and member, some were distributed to the railway companies and others were sent to our immigration agents in England and in the United States.
Are the visitors to Banff increasing ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed they are increasing very largely.
Principally Americans.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
From every country.

Where was this work done ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The drawing of the maps Is done in the geographer's office, Ottawa, and the Toronto Lithographing Company does the printing.
Is it let by contract ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am given to understand there is only one company in Canada that *does copper engraving.

We did get some maps printed in Chicago and they were done very cheaply. I would prefer having them done in our own country if we could get them at a reasonable price, but it does seem to me there ought to be competition in these contracts, especially when they are for large amounts.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are certain classes of work that Canada is not as far advanced in as other countries, and this appears to be one of them. If we invite competition it would simply be competition between our own country and other countries.
That was done before.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and it may have been the better way, but there has been considerable feeling expressed against giving so much government money to foreign industries, ^rat it was thought if we could get the work at a moderate price we should keep the work in our own country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I suppose, with regard to the large map of the Dominion, the printing is done in many thousands, while the mounting is done only in comparatively small numbers as required, on account of the greater expense of mounting.
How are these maps distributed ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no definite system of distribution. They are issued to members who apply for them, and members generally apply for them for use in schools, and it is thought desirable to have such maps used in the schools.

If there are maps or other things given to members for distribution in schools or anywhere else, all the members ought to be furnished with a list of such things ; otherwise those who have opportunity of knowing about them get what they want, while others are left without them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think this might be done ; while the department might print the maps for general information, those who desire to have them mounted might very well be asked to pay the cost of mounting.

This is a large expense merely for the distribution of these maps by members among their constituents. The man who knows about them gets them, while the man who does not know about them does not get any. I would have no objection to a senator or a member getting one of these maps ; but to use them in a way as perquisites to members who apply for them is not what we are here for, and not what we ought, to spend the people's money for. This matter was brought to my attention by a letter which I received

from an old friend in New Brunswick, who said that So-and-so had sent flue mounted maps to three or four of his friends in that locality, but that he could not get one, and he wanted me to get one for him. I have not applied for it, because I did not know whether I could get one or not. I would have some sympathy with allowing every member to have three or four of these maps if they went into schools. To furnish maps to every school in the country is a large undertaking, and if you furnish to one why not to another. To make these expensive maps and give them to members as a piece of patronage to be circulated among their constituents is not good public policy. A simpler and less expensive way, would be to let each member have a half a dozen or so unmounted maps and pay for the mounting themselves. I do not see how you could get these mounted maps through the mails.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I quite agree that we should arrive at some sound basis of distribution. Evidently the House considers it desirable to provide such maps for the use of the schools, unmounted if not mounted. If a charge were made for the mounting, that would be a considerable check on the demand for the mounted maps. There is no difficulty about sending the mounted maps because they are sent by express. They can be mounted in large numbers much cheaper and better than they could by the individual.

Prince Edward Island Railway-dwelling for agent at Bloomfield, $715.
Is that outside of the station house ?
That is outside of the station house.

I would like to know what the policy of the government is in reference to that, whether it is proposed now to commence and build dwelling houses for the agents. The hon. minister will see that if there is a dwelling house built for one agent in one place there will be demands upon him for dwelling houses for agents in other places. The expense of one house is small, but if this is going to be taken as the policy of the government it is going to add an immense sum to the obligations of a railway which is now not paying. It does not seem to show anything but a backward tendency under the hou. gentleman's management.

I quite agree with the idea that my hon. friend is throwing out with regard to the construction of dwellings. Certainly St is not the policy of the department to construct dwellings except where it is absolutely necessary ; that is where the station is situated so that it is impossible for the agent to secure a residence near the scene of his work It is important to have the agent always right near the station. In the olden time on the Intercolonial Railway7, or rather before it became the Intercolonial Railway, they started out building station houses that included dwellings upstairs for the agents. There is quite a number of these, as my hon. friend very well knows, between Moncton and St. John on what is now known as the

Intercolonial Railway, but which was known as the European and North American Railway in days gone by. That was necessary because in establishing stations as they did they were unable to do so in settled communities and the station agent could not get a dwelling house. The policy is gradually changing and in constructing new stations we eliminate the dwelling house feature in almost every instance, but where it is impossible for the agent to secure a dwelling by rental near the station we find it necessary to build a dwelling house for him adjoining the station. We sometimes utilize an old building. These conditions prevail in Prince Edward Island, as I am advised, and it is necessary at this place, and I think at some other places on the island to which my attention has been invited, to do this. It is done upon the report of the officials. It is purely departmental and it is only done where it is necessary. The general policy of the department is not to furnish dwellings. If we furnish a dwelling, of course the officials get the benefit of it ; but those who are not so favoured receive compensation in lieu of it ; that is to say, an allowance is made for the rental paid for them. There is no discrimination. All are treated alike and it is regulated by agreement with the Telegrapher's Union, which comprises amongst its membership the station agents along the line of the Intercolonial Railway and Prince Edward Island Railway
Is Bloomfield in an utterly unsettled portion of the country in Prince Edward Island ?

Gratuity to Jeffrey Foot, ex-tide waiter, Halifax, $500.

Mr. Jeffrey Foot was appointed a tide waiter in His Majesty's customs at the port of Halifax, Nova Scotia, on the 1st February, 1895, at a salary of $500 per annum. His age at the time of appointment was 53 years so that he did not come within the provisions of the Superannuation Act-the age limit provided by such Act being 45 years. On the 22nd January, 1903, while acting as locker at warehouse No. 14, of the port of Halifax, Mr. Foot met with an accident which greatly aggravated a disease from which he was suffering and in consequence he was permanently disabled. While discharging his duties on the day referred to a teamster came driving along at a rapid rate, the shaft of the wagon knocked Mr. Foot down, he was trampled by the horse and the wagon passed over him. His head was badly cut and he was unconscious for a considerable time. He has made a statutory declaration setting forth the cause of the accident as before stated and the circumstances as narrated are verified by affidavits of Mr. A. S. Taylor, a clerk, and Mr. A. O. Gastonguay, a merchant, who were eye witnesses of the accident. The Department of Customs gave Mr. Foot the only relief possible under the law, which was payment of his salary for 12 months. Section 10 of the Civil Service Superannuation Act provides that if any officer is constrained to quit the service be-

fore the period of superannuation, ten years, by reason of severe bodily injury, received without -his own fault, in the discharge of his public duty, the Governor in Council may allow him a gratuity not exceeding three months pay for every two years service. Taking into account the extra year during which Mr. Foot was paid as a public officer his service would only amount to nine years or one year less than the period covered by the Civil Service Act. On the basis provided in section 10 of the Superannuation Act the gratuity to be allowed Mr. Foot would be $500, namely : three months salary at $500 per annum, $125, multiplied by 4 as his full service was 4| times 2 years service.

River St. Lawrence ship channel, Marine Department-further amount required on account of the construction of a dredge for improvement of the channel below Quebec, $100,000.
Mr. PREF0NTAINE. This amount is required for immediate disbursements on account of material and labour towards the construction of a sea-going, steel, twin-screw, suction, hopper dredge for improvements to the river -St. Lawrence ship channel below Quebec, to be constructed at the government works at Sorel. Estimated cost, $350,000. The thirty foot channel at low water between Quebec and Montreal is now well on towards completion. In two or three years we will have vessels sailing between Montreal and Quebec at all stages of the tide, while below Quebec there is at one place only 20 feet at low tide. In the spring of 1901 the matter was brought to the attention of the Minister of Public Works by the shipping interest of Montreal. The officers of the Marine and Fisheries Department of Quebec, who had an intimate knowledge of this part of the river, strongly recommended the north channel, commencing below the Island of Orleans, as being better, easier navigated and more clear of ice in winter. Orders were given to the staff of the River St. Lawrence ship channel to make a survey and examination of the north channel with ** view to reporting on the practicability and cost of improving that route and adopting it for navigation. In 1902 a similar survey was made of the south channel to ascertain what improvements would be required to make a thirty foot channel on the line of the present route.
A comprehensive report was made on February 24, 1903, to the acting chief engineer of the Public Works Department on the question of the proposed improvement below Quebec. The engineer, who is now superintending engineer of the work being carried out on the St. Lawrence by this department, Mr. Cowie, reported that the difficulties by either route are between Murray hay and St. Jean, Isle d'Orleans. The dredger required for either would be practically the same, the material everywhere being soft.
It was estimated that for either route, the * cost, including the required plant, to give a thirty foot channel. 1.000 feet wide, would be about $1,000,000, and it was urged that immediate steps should be taken to provide the dredge, as it would require a year and a half to build. Mr. Cowie did not recommend the adoption of either route, but advised that the choice should meet with the

approval of the underwriters, the shipping interest and the pilots. The decision as to the route need not he given at once. The Transportation Commission visited the locality, going over each channel and took evidence on the subject, and it is hoped that they will go further into the question and give an opinion. In the meantime the superintending engineer has submitted the proposal that the plant be constructed and the present south channel dredged to thirty feet and to a width of say 500 feet. This could be done, it is estimated, in two seasons. Then, if considered advisable, the dredging of the north channel Traverse shoals could be undertaken.
How much has been expended ?

Not a cent yet, but we are figuring on ordering the necessary material in order to start the work. The work will be done at the Sorel shipyards. It will be one of the most modern and improved dredges.
A suction dredge ?
A suction and hopper dredge at the same time.
The hon. gentleman spoke of the Transportation Commission having visited this locality, did they make any suggestion or report ?

They made a report which I have not before me. It stands to reason that if you have a thirty foot channel between Montreal and Quebec, you must also have a thirty foot channel between Quebec and the Gulf, and there are shoals at different points below Quebec where the water is only twenty feet deep at low tide.
When do you expect to complete the dredge ?
In eighteen months.
Then how long will it take to dredge the channel ?

In two seasons the work will be done in the south channel because we will be able to get the help of other dredges now working between Montreal and Quebec. We have seven dredges finishing the work between Montreal and Quebec, and in eighteen months we shall be able to take away two or three of them and use them in the south channel below Quebec. After the south channel is dredged, we will work in the north channel.
These two channels continue only a portion of the distance ?

About thirty-five miles. One is on the north side of the island of Orleans and the other is on the south side. In days gone by, the north channel was the one used, but at that time
vessels had not the draught they have now. The south channel was then adopted and greatly improved ; but at two points near Murray bay and Beauchemin, there are . shoals where the water at low tide is only twenty feet. This means a delay of six or seven hours when steamers strike' those points at low water.
What is the rise and the fall of the tide ?
About 18 feet.
This will give two channels, and it is contemplated that each will be a 3(Moot channel ?
Yes, at the lowest point.
The minimum depth. And what will be the minimum width ?

Five hundred feet. The north channel, when completed, will be about a mile. It is very deep water, except at certain points. There is very little to lie done on the north channel, except at the northeast end of the island of Orleans.

The hon. minister (Mr. Prgfontaine) spoke of the Transportation Commission. We do not hear very much about that commission now. It began its work, I think, about two years ago this summer. But we have not had the advantage of its wisdom, except that upon one occasion, I think, they made a short report with regard to some particular locality. There is danger that we shall have completed all our arrangements with respect to the matters this commission was to investigate before we receive its report. And it would be most unfortunate if it should advise something altogether different from the measures we are now engaged in carrying out. Of course, it is quite possible-as great minds think alike-that the government may be proceeding exactly along the lines which the Transportation Commission will eventually advise. But will it not he possible for the government to stimulate the activity of the commission a little, and so enable us, some time before the end of the present century, to find out what it is doing or what it advises ?

This Transportation Commission, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) is aware, is not under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, but is under the control of the Department of Public Works. I must admit there has been a good deal of delay, hut it is due to circumstances over which we had no control. As he knows, one of the [DOT]gentlemen on that commission was sick for a long time and died a few months ago. Another member of the commission, Mr. Fry, of Quebec, resigned a few months ago. The work of the commission was suspended

because of these things. As to the work *which pertains to my department-the work of the ship channel-I must say that every . time we were in doubt as to what should be done, I gave Mr. Cowie, the engineer in charge, instructions to consuu with them. Everything we are doing as to the ship channel proper has received the approval of the commission. Of course, in years past there was much careful study of the St. Lawrence channel and its needs by the engineers of the Department of Public Works ; and, on any points that may have been in doubt, though our engineers had their own opinion formed as regards these points, Mr. Cowie has always acted with due care, and I am quite sure that any work he has recommended, and which is in process of being carried out, will be found to be such that it need not be done over again. The plan has been carefully thought out. These improvements will be finished within four or five years. Then, if the question arises of further widening or deepening of the channel, the public, especially those interested in transportation and navigation, will find that no mistakes have been made. The work has been efficiently carried on under my predecessor as Minister of Public Works, and, since it has been under my charge, I have given it my personal attention. These works have received the unanimous approval of those connected with navigation. We have been pressed by the boards of trade, the shipping federation and other similar bodies to carry out the work as fast as possible so as to meet the demands of our commerce.

In answer to the hou. leader of the opposition, I may say that I do not know what the commission has done since the beginning of this session ; my impression is that they have done nothing, by reason of the resignation of one of the members and of the death of another. As I have said, the commission is not under my control, though of course I am a member of the government under whose control it is. I must state also that the works which pertain to the ship channel were decided upon and were carried out without the aid of the commission, except in one or two eases where they were consulted by the superintending engineer with regard to certain improvements. The improvements of the channel were decided upon, and have been carried on, even before the commission was appointed. I understand that the scope of the commission was mostly to consider the question of transportation as regards the great lakes, transportation by water as well as by rail. It was especially for that purpose that the commission was appointed. Of course, in special cases they may have been called upon to examine certain points, they may have been sitting as experts on certain improvements, such as improvements contemplated in the har-bous of St. John, as well as in the harbour of Halifax and other places. But with regard to the ship channel, I state again that the plan of improvement was laid out a number of years ago, and was matured before the commission was appointed. The commission only pronounced on this ship channel between Montreal and Quebec, as well as between Quebec and the Gulf, in cases where there may have been some doubt as regards the best locality in which to make the improvements. posed for starting the dumping of the material, the flushing to be done by the main centrifugal pump. excavation of canals or the construction of railways.
