I need not tell the minister how that thing is done. In the first place, they come to the House and ask for an appropriation, they commend a certain kind of work. If the House approves of the work and votes the money, then it becomes the duty of the department to give effect to that resolution by carrying out the work. If parliament says m its wisdom that the work is not desirable, or that the cost is going to be too great, then, of course, they refuse the appropriation, and that will be an instruction to the minister not to continue that particular work. Now, the minister has intimated that in some way this is connected with a previous vote. If so, it is something that the House has not heard of at all, at any rate It is a very vague connection, and the minister cannot justify himself in committing tlie country to an expenditure of $115,000, when, by bringing down an estimate at any time after tbe 15tk of January last, lie could, if it was a feasible work, have obtained the sanction of parliament, and could have gone on in the regular constitutional way to expend the money. Here we are in tlie month of May, after being in session for nearly five months, and we are told that the minister lias decided to do a certain work, that it is going to cost $115,000, that he has called for tenders and the work is practically going on. Of necessity it will have to be finished by the SOtli of June, otherwise this vote will not be available! Now. I think we are getting too much of this kind of thing, and I trust the minister will not humiliate the House to tlie extent he has been doing in tbe past. This occurs every year in the departments. The House is practically told that they are merely here to register the acts of the government, not to be consulted, not to be taken into the confidence of tlie government and asked whether this expenditure is reasonable or not, whether tbe country can afford it or not. but simply to register what they in their majestic minds think it to their advantage to do as a political party. I hope the minister will not ask us to" vote any more estimates like this ; if he does, I shall be obliged again to draw the attention of tbe House -to the fact that such a mode of expending the people's money is not a constitutional mode.

I can relieve the anxiety of my hon. friend. As regards the Beaujeu bank, tbe work was contemplated and mentioned during the discussion of tlie Mr. HENIUSRSON.
estimates last year. As a matter of fact, that work has been going on since September of last year. Fortunately, that was included in the general expense of construction of aids to navigation. There was no special vote for the Beaujeu bank, but it was among tbe improvements contemplated. The expenditure of the department has been large, but tlie department has not done worse than other departments, it has striven to do the best possible with the amount available at its disposal. The work had to go on. It was contemplated in the ship channel vote, for which there was an amount of $80,000. We thought we would not be doing anything against the constitution or against tlie public interest in taking advantage of a number of men being out of work and putting them to work at Sorel in tbe shipyard, preparing for tbe installation of these piers, so that they could be finished at the end of this seasoif. If we had not done so, we would probably have lost one season. Part of the work bad to be done under water, and it had to be finished before the close of navigation. So that really we do not deserve the censure of the hon. gentleman. This is one of those works that, when started. must go on, even if there is no money voted by -parliament, because otherwise tbe country would suffer loss if the work was not done at the time and in the manner contemplated. If we have a vote of half a million dollars and, in going on with the work that was contemplated when we made that estimate, we exceed the amount, the general practice is that we come before tbe House and ask for so much additional for that work. I could have done that easily if I had wanted to mislead the House. I could have stated that in order to complete the work of the ship channel as contemplated by tbe expenditure which was asked last year $115,000 was necessary ; but no. I wanted tbe House and tbe country to know what we were doing in improving the channel. so that nothing would be done in the dark. Probably it would have passed easier if I had just stated that the $115,000 was required to complete the work of the ship channel. On the contrary, I came openly before tbe House, and I think I should be given credit for acting openly in the interests of tlie public.

I am sure we will all give tbe bon. minister credit for boldness in- acting openly. Even when he gets very far astray he is not afraid to do that. He tells us that this is a continuation of the work for which an appropriation was obtained last year under tbe beading ' Aids to Navigation.'

Last year there was a good deal of distinction made between Aids to Navigation and the ship channel. Tlie ship channel was not under my control until the 1st of July, so that this amount for piers on lake St. Peter was
*6457

supposed to be paid out of the amount of -$500,000 voted for the ship channel. The work at Beaujeu bank was contemplated to be paid for out of the vote for aids to navigation. In order to make it clearer we have put the item in such a way that everybody can understand it.

If the hon. minister himself understands it nobody else in this House does. I think he has mystifyed the matter as much as possible. He commenced a work part of which he tells us is being paid for out of the vote obtained for the purpose of improving the ship channel while another portion is being paid for out of money which, was voted for aids to navigation. Then he comes down with apparently a new item entirely for the construction of works we never heard of before :
To provide for permanent piers in Lake St. Peter and other places in the ship channel, including Beaujeu bank, $115,000.
How can any lion, member of the committee connect that with the estimates that were asked for and voted last year ? For my part I never would have suspected that there was any connection whatever, and I think the hon. minister is drawing upon his imagination very largely when he attempts to make this connection. It seems to me that it is rather an after thought. It is one of those adroit methods he has of pulling the wool over the eyes of the members of this House when he gets into a tight corner. I give him credit for that. He is an adept at that sort of thing, but notwithstanding that I stick to what I said before. This seems to me to be an entirely new item, something which has originated since we last met in parliament, something that was not provided for in the session of last year and something which should not have been undertaken until this vote was *obtained and the consent of the House also obtained to the expenditure of the money. The reason I have made reference to it is because we find that there is a great tendency year after year to expend money regardless of the feelings of the members of this House, without considering whether "the country approves of it and without regard in fact to any kind of economy. How is the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) going to provide means for carrying on the affairs of this country if the ministers in the various departments are going to proceed with the construction of works of which he has no knowledge and of which he has no information at the time lie makes his estimates for the expenditures of the year ? It seems to me that it is heaping a great deal of trouble on the hon. minister whose duty it is to provide .all the money that is necessary for carrying on the affairs of the country. To my mind it is not treating that hon. gentleman with fairness, and I hope the day will come when he will call his colleagues to account
and ask them to be good enough to confine themselves to what parliament has voted in the expenditure of the money of this country and not continuously to draw upon the future for funds which the hon. Minister of Finance has had no opportunity of providing.

The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. I'refontaine) says that he has been spending money and that he wants the country to know what he is doing and what he has done with its money. Well, I may tell the hon. minister that the country does not care a cent for information of that character. Every year items of this kind come before the House ; we are tormented almost to death with items of $50,000, $150,000 or $200,000 and every hon. minister appears to have a good reason for paying out the people's money. I tell you that the country does not care a cent when a statement of that kind is made to it. You know what was done a few years ago with the money which this House voted for the Seven Islands scheme. What can you call that ? Then, we had the Grande Yallfie scheme. I would ask the hon. minister not to imagine that the people are anxious to be told of expenditures of that kind. They are not, and if the hon. minister thinks they are he is greatly mistaken. The country does not care to hear of them and they do not like to pay for them. These hon. gentlemen expend half a million here or $300,000 there and then when we call attention to it we are criticised from the other side because, as these hon. gentlemen say, we are detaining the House. Well. I say gentlemen you are the servants of the people and you are no more than the clerks of the people. You have the Minister of Finance to collect the money for you, he pays it out to you and then you go and pay it out to your Grit friends all over the country. That is just the way it stands. In all these works that you propose to do and particularly in connection with this dredge, there will not be a Tory employed. It will be a Grit shop and a Grit dredge. If a Tory goes there and asks for work he will be told that there is none. It is just the same as it is on the Transcontinental Railway, or on the Grand Trunk Pacific as we call it sometimes. A Conservative cannot get work on the Transcontinental Railway. The government will send to New York and engage Italians and Hungarians rather than give a white man work. That is the way the government tries to blindfold us ; they are spending half a million a year doing work on that ship channel and it has got to be a farce. Formerly they were dredging between Montreal and Quebec but now they are dredging away down the gulf, and they are spending money building dredges that are fit to go to London. We have a right to complain of this and we will continue to complain until the government give up doing wrong.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: This item is ' to provide permanent piers in Lake St. Peter and other places in the ship channel.' How many piers are to be erected in Lake St. Peter and how many elsewhere ?

' There are four in Lake St. Peter, which will cost more than the $78,000 in this vote, and will have to be provided for as to the balance in the supplementary estimates cfor next year. X think the report of the engineer states that he contemplates putting piers at each bend of the river, which would be about eight or nine altogether.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You say there are four to be erected in Lake St. Peter : where are the others ?
They are not to be built out of this amount of $78,000, which will not cover the expenditure on the four piers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: There was nothing said about these piers last year, and therefore this is the first time that the question has been brought before the House. The minister has undertaken work which was never approved of by parliament, and that system must be condemned.
The item of $581,000 last year for the ship channel had in view the establishment of these piers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We do not know what it had in view, but we heard nothing about these piers.
I cannot tell what was stated by the Minister of Public Works, who asked for the vote last year, but probably no details were asked from him.
You contracted for jobs that were not approved by parliament.
It was approved by parliament.
How could it be approved by parliament when we never heard anything about it 1
There are lots of things approved by parliament that you hear nothing about.
They are approved in your mind, and the people have to pav for them.

In the item of $o80,000 many works were included, probably two or three hundred items, and if the minister were not asked about each item he probably would only mention the most important, which was for the dredging. I had a list before me this year, and if I were asked I would have given each item which made up the $580,000, and I suppose the same thing was done last vear when the $581,000 was voted for the ship channel.

This year I took the precaution of putting in the item to read ' River St. Lawrence ship channel, Marine Department,' and as there was need of $115,000 more for the ship channel, I explained how the money would be expended to the 1st July.
The expression ' ship channel ' is misleading.
I did not invent it.

Where ignorance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise. When you speak of a ship channel, it means to the ordinary mind that you are dredging that channel, but you are now using this money to build permanent docks.
These are permanent piers to install lights at the bends of the river.
Then it is for lighting the channel ?
It is always considered as part of the ship channel.
It has no connection with the making of the channel at all, and therefore the expression is misleading.
All works pertaining to the channel have been considered as ship channel works.

For my part, I cannot see that these piers will be any help whatever to navigation. I have seen the St. Lawrence below Quebec clear of ice as late as the 27th day of December, and yet navigation had been closed for over a month. When the time comes for navigation to close in the fall of the year the ships will cease to go up the St. Lawrence, and this expenditure is simply a waste of money.
When were these contracts let ?

There is only one contract let. We simply prepared the crib-work preparatory to the installation of the piers, and the four piers are being erected by day's work. The first pier was included in the expenditure last year under the head of ' aids to navigation.' Tenders were asked in September last year, and the contract was let some time afterwards. It was for $25,000, which was the lowest tender.
That was let about the time of the general election.

No, I think it was after the general election. At any rate, it does not make much difference ; there was not enough difference to kill a cat. Public tenders were asked through the newspapers, and there were only two tenders, one of $25,500 and the other $25,000.
Mr. BLAIN, Who was the successful tenderer ?

Mr. PREFONT AINK- Crevier & Lemoine. The other was Dussault & Lemieux.
When is the work to he completed ?

1 think by the 1st of September. The contract was given at the end of the season in order to give the men a chance to prepare their cribwork in the winter ; but nothing , is to be paid until the crib is sunk and put in place.
Why could not all the cribwork for the different lights be let by tender ?	.
We thought it was better to employ our men of the shipyard at Sore] to prepare these piers in the winter on the ice. We thought it was more economical.
The cribs are prepared by the government employees, and the filling is done by contract ?

No filling in is given out bv contract. We intend to do the concrete work. The steel superstructure will of course be done partly by the shipyard and perhaps partly outside ; I do not know exactly. But the four piers on Lake ist. Peter we intend to stall by day labour as much as possible.
Where is the material obtained with which you fill the cribwork ?
By public tender. There is rough stone for filling and broken stone for concrete, all got by public tender.

Where is the material
obtained ?
The lumber has been obtained at different places. I can give the hon. gentleman a complete list of the different tenderers. The cement has not been delivered yet.
I wanted to know where the broken stone was obtained.
I do not know where it is obtained, but a man named Beauchemin of Sorel is the lowest tenderer. The price is $1.80 a ton.
Do you buy broken stone by the ton or by the yard ?
By the ton.
It seems a very peculiar way.
Does the contract specify that the broken stone shall be bought by the ton instead of by the cord ?
I never heard of stone being bought by the cord. Toise, the hon. gentleman means. The cord is not a legal measure in the province of Quebec.

That is news to me. I understand that it is bought by the cord in other provinces, and it seems to me that is the proper way to buy stone for cribwork. Do the specifications call for stone of any particular quarry ?
We do not care where the stone comes from so long as it is good and acceptable.
I am simply asking for information. The government, then, does not specify any particular quarry ?
No.
I never before heard of stone being bought by the ton. Would the minister give us an idea of what a yard of stone weighs or what a ton measures ? .
A yard weighs a little over a ton and a half.
And the price of $1.80 a ton is equivalent to $2.70 per cubic yard. I am sure the electors of this country will not like to hear the price of that stone.
I think they will.
I think the man who has the quarry will be delighted, but the minister has been led very far astray in regard to the price of broken stone.
I may say that a week ago I bought some at the same price for my own use.
This was large stone for cribwork ?
Stone broken by machinery for making concrete.
The gentleman who has that contract has a bonanza far better than the Klondike.
What facilities were afforded at this particular place for weighing the stone ?
It was weighed with a scale.

The minister said, in answer to a question firom this !side of the House, that this item of $llo,000 would not be used for other places than those on Lake St. Peter, and yet as the item reads, the whole of it might be used elsewheie. If the minister's explanation is correct, i ii,o ntiipr words should be struck out.
I am satisfied ; let them be struck out.
If I figure the price out rightly, it will amount to $12 per cord. The average price in Ontario w7ould be about $4 per cord of 128 cubic yards.

I do not know of any measure of that kind.
*6463

I have had a good deal of experience in contracts, including government contracts, and I never heard of such a price paid for stone in my experience as that paid toy the government in this instance.
Compensation in full and final settlement of all claims to the heirs of the late Joseph Paul, of the hydraulic dredge ' Jos. Israel Tarte,' who was accidentally killed by the explosion of a boiler November 3, 1903, $4,000.
How is it that this has been standing so long ?

This session there was an investigation before the Public Accounts Committee to ascertain the cause of the accident. It was ascertained that there was no defect in the boiler but that the explosion was due to the carelessness of one of those who were killed. The Department of Justice held that consequently the government were responsible to the heirs of this man and recommended a settlement in the following manner. $1,000 was paid to the widow and $3,000 paid to tutors in trust for the children.
Does the hon. minister expect a similar claim from the blowing up of the Scout ?
I think we will be obliged to pay something. When the Item for repairs and expenses of service, item 87, comes up, I will be in a position to give full information as regards the claim.
Is the investigation over ?

Yes.
Further amount required for maintenance and repairs to Dominion steamers and ice breakers, $75,000.

The amount voted for maintenance and repairs to Dominion steamers last year was $375,000. Since then two steamers, the ' Montcalm ' and ' Champlain,' have been added to the fleet. The expenditure to the 30th April was $318,252, leaving a balance to the credit of the appropriation of $7,009. This balance has been held over for the payment of the wages of the crews, and in consequence there has been an accumulation of accounts for maintenance and repairs. The department has now four ice breakers in commission during the winter, and the fuel consumption of these steamers is very large. There is also a balance due for repairs to the 1 Lady Laurier.' It will be remembered that this ship met with an accident going to the harbour at Lockeport and immediate repairs had to be made. Part of the cost was paid out of the appropriation of 1903-4 and the balance out of the appropriation for the current year. This was an altogether unforeseen accident and was charged to the vote for maintenance. The * Stanley ' and * Minto ' had also to have large repairs to machinery and engines to get them ready

for the winter's work. The * Stanley's ' boilers were retubed and extra propeller blades imported from the builders for both these ships. The amount asked for will bring the appropriation this year up to $400,000, the same amount as is asked for next year. Last year it was pointed out that $325,000 would not be sufficient.

The minister will remember that on the 20th February I asked for a return with reference to supplies ordered by circular in connection with the maintenance of these Dominion steamers. That return is not yet down.
I inquired tltis morning if all these papers had been laid before the House and was told they had been. I shall make further inquiry and bring down any that may be missing.
I understand that a return was ordered on the 13th February concerning the purchase of supplies and on the 20th February a similar return was ordered. Those two have not yet been brought down.
If not, I shall bring them down before getting through my estimates.
The cost of maintaining these steamers is growing pretty fast-at the rate of $100,000 every year. Last year it was $306,094 and now it is $400,000.
The number of the steamers has increased also. Formerly we had only one ice breaker and now we have four.
Is this $75,000 in addition to the $325,000 previously voted and will it enable the department to reach the end of the current fiscal year without any deficit ?
Yes.
Will the hon. minister give a little information as to the success of the experiment of sending an ice-breaker to Newfoundland to assist in-coming vessels ?

The ' Montcalm ' was sent to Newfoundland to help steamers coming in, but unfortunately none of these steamers which were coming in had any Marconi apparatus on board and the apparatus was not working at the station. Therefore the ' Montcalm ' was not able to get communication with the other steamers so as to be able to assist them. So, really, the trip was of no effect on account of there being no Marconi system on ships coming in.
Ocean and river service-to orovide for the construction of new boilers and repairs to hull of steamer ' Aberdeen,' $17,000.

Late last fall when the ' Aberdeen ' came into winter quarters in Quebec we found that her boil-

ers were out of order and had to be entirely renewed. We asked for and received a tender for the work from the Poison Iron Works. The tender was considered reasonable and we sent the boat to Toronto. She is being fitted with the boilers and is expected to be ready in two weeks.
Were tenders advertised for in the public press ?

No, they were a special	boiler,-Thorney croft Watertube
boiler. Nobody but the Poisons could tender for them. Had we not done this we should have been obliged to send the steamer to England. The tender received was considered reasonable and was so reported by the special expert, the late Douglas Stevens.
What could be the object of asking for tenders, when as the minister says there was only one firm ? And this is another case where the contract was entered into before the money was voted.
More of that.
Oh, that is becoming quite common with this government.

Would the hon. gentleman expect us to delay until the vote was passed and so lose the whole summer of the boat and be obliged to hire another boat to do the work ? I think that -would be rather poor policy on the part of the department.
Does the department allow its steamers to get into such a condition that they are likely to explode so that the renewal of boilers becomes a matter of emergency ?
It was a matter of emergency.

If so, it is no wonder that we have explosions such as that in the case of the ' Scout.' We have boilers that are allowed to get into such condition that they cannot do their work and then the government must order renewals before the money is voted, instead of keeping boilers properly inspected and arranging for expenditures in due time.

The boilers were properly inspected. As 1 have stated it was the end of the season and our officers thought the boilers should be renewed. We took the precaution to have them renewed so that the boat would be ready soon after the opening of navigation. Had it not been that the boat was delayed in the Soulanges canal by the ice she would have been ready now. Unfortunately she was caught in the ice, and we had to wait until the 1st of May to send her to Toronto to get the work done. The work is being done and will be completed in a fortnight.

It seems to me that this method of spending money before it is
voted by parliament could be avoided by the several departments by including in their estimates a certain sum for unforeseen emergencies, to be expended by them at the discretion of the council. I think that would be much preferable to the system of calling for the money after it has been illegally spent. I am sure this House would be willing to vote a sum to each department that might be used to meet unforeseen emergencies. Parliament undoubtedly has the right to declare in advance whether the money shall be spent, and no cabinet, and no minister has the right to spend money which has not been voted.

I concur in the suggestion made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ames). The spending departments of the government have been considering such a scheme, though we have not yet perfected it. It is a most awkward thing when, at the end of the season, some unforeseen expenditure becomes necessary. It is always open to all sorts of criticism. If we could come to such an understanding as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ames) suggests, it would be in the interest of the public and of the department.
in the face of an unforeseen emergency making expenditure necessary, the department can always fall back upon a Governor General's warrant.

I think the House was in session when we wanted the money.
Mr. SI'ROUTE. In such a case, parliament can be applied to for a vote.
It would take too long ; it would lose the whole season.

I do not think that the government would be justified in drawing upon the public exchequer when the parliament is in session. The House never refuses to vote money if there is urgent need for it.
Ocean and river service-further amount required for investigations into wrecks, $2,000.
Is this for additional salaries and, if so, to whom is it to be paid ?

No, it is not for salaries. Parliament, voted $2,000, but the expenditure has been $4,317.95.
To pay Captain James Harrison, master of the steamship ' Grecian,' an allowance for expenses incurred by him in connection with the investigation into the stranding of the ship in Halifax harbour on February 19th, 1902, $750.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why is this ?

About two years ago an investigation was held in connection with the loss of the ss. ' Grecian ' at Halifax. At the inquiry held Captain James Harrison's certificate was cancelled, but be subsequently went to England and appealed and his certificate was returned to him.
This service cost more last year than usual on account of the severity of the winter and the increased difficulty of navigation between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.

Is the minister making any extra preparations for the coming winter ? It is contended that all was not done last winter that could have been done in order to convey the mails backwards and forwards. that there was negligence on the part of the authorities. As we' have no reason to suppose that the winters are getting any milder, I would like to know if there is any way of improving this service in order Mr. PREFONTAINE.
to make it more effective than it has been j in the past ?

Last winter was more severe than usual, and navigation was interrupted a longer time than in any other year in the history of navigation between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. There was no negligence on the part of the captains of the steamers, and no one has ever charged them with negligence ; they did the best they could under the circumstances.
Further amount required for the extension of the coast service and surveys on the north and northwest coasts of Canada, $65,000.
This is a very large item, and we would like some explanation. Is there some new expedition to be fitted out, or is it a continuation of what is already in existence ?

It is a continuation of the expenditure connected with the expedition of the ' Arctic ' last year. We shall have to send a boat with coal, provisions and men to join the ' Arctic.' This boat is supposed to leave in June and return by tbe end of July, bringing back some of the men who are sick and disabled. She will also carry some men to complete the equipment of the ' Arctic ' and to station at the posts.
Mr. I-IENDERSO'N. It seems to me we are spending a large amount of money in that region. I am not complaining of the amount at all, but it would be interesting to the House if reports somewhat extended could be given to the House that we may know the result of this expedition.
If the hon. gentleman will turn to the report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries he will find an extensive report by Mr. bow, made on his return last year.

I am much obliged to the hon. gentleman for drawing my attention to that. I had not seen it. I was looking rather for some special report. Anything we can learn about that northern country will be of great interest.
If the hon. gentleman will take communication of that report he will get a great deal of information, because it is very elaborate and complete.

May I ask the minister how far northward the ' Arctic ' has gone ? Is there any attempt to get away into the region of the North Pole, so as to take possession of the islands lying north of the continent of North America, in the name of the King, and setting aside for ever any claim that the United States or some other country may make in that region of the world ? We desire to avoid any complications such as we had in the case of Alaska. Is this expedition commanded by Captain Bernier ?
Captain Bernier is the sailing master of the ' Arctic,' the expedition is commanded by Major Moodie.

I have certainly a great deal of confidence in Cajitain Bernier's ability to sail those northern waters, or to sail waters in almost any part of the world.
I think it is a great pity that the government did not avail itself some years ago of the services of Captain Bernier ill exploring the northern regions of the continent of America. Even had they granted him the assistance which he came and pleaded for year after year, with a view to make that final effurt to discover the North Pole, and thus advertise Canada all over the world, I think the government could have spent $100,000 with a great deal of satisfaction in that direction. We are now spending hundreds of thousands of dollars in surveying a portion of the coast of North America, which I think will bring very much less of interest to the people of this country than would have resulted from an expedition toward the Pole with a view of making that long coveted discovery. Now, here is $65,000 this year. If I mistake not, this expenditure already has gone up to the hundreds of thousands. As I said, I am not complaining about it. I think perhaps it may be money well spent, if it will be the means of preventing complications between ourselves and our neighbours to the south of us, who are also pushing out in that direction with a view to claiming something in these northern regions which we may not have laid our hands upon. I simply express my regret that the services of Captain Bernier were not obtained years ago, and that he was not placed at the head of an expedition that would once for all have settled the question of who was entitled to the sovereignty of those islands lying between the North Pole and the presently known continent of North America.

This is an item of $65,-
000.	Will this be in addition to the amount which we voted last year for the same ex pedition ?

This is supplementary.
5Ir. SPROULE. Yes.

The sum of $170,000 was transferred from the Northwest Mounted Police to the Department of Marine and Fisheries for the Hudson bay expedition. Out of that amount the department paid $29,018. balance due the High Commissioner in London for the purchase of the steamer ' Gauss.' afterwards called the * Arctic.' The total sum paid for the ' Arctic ' was $70,000 and $40,982 was paid out of the appropriation for 1903-04. The balance of the amount transferred from the Northwest Mounted Police was expended in fitting out the ' Erik ' as a relief steamer for
the ' Neptune.' The ' Erik ' was charted from Job Brothers & Company, St. John's, to take coal and supplies to the ' Neptune.' The ' Arctic ' was fitted out and provisioned at Quebec and it was found that the funds at the disposal of the government were not suflicient to meet the expenditure. Besides the ' Arctic,' the department had to make repairs to the ' Neptune ' after it returned to Halifax. The ' Neptune ' unfortunately met with an accident coming out of Hudson bay and the department was obliged to place the ship on the marine slip at Halifax for repairs. It was found besides damages to the bow that part of the keel was knocked off and other damages were sustained which required to be renewed. The amount asked for is required to meet all liabilities in connection with the expedition up to the 30th June.
As regards the remarks made by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) that we should have given charge of the expedition to Captain Bernier, I beg to disagree. The question of these expeditions was discussed two years ago and the first expedition was sent out under the charge of Mr. Low. It was composed of a certain number of members of the Northwest. Mounted Police, because the government thought they should establish a post up there. Mr. Low made a report of the work he did and a certain number of mounted police were left there. While he was up there we thought we would send a boat, the Arctic,' up for three years to survey and visit the different points in Hudson bay, to go as far north as possible under the orders of Major Moodie, establish posts at different places, make researches, gather information and establish customs offices at different points because there is a great- deal of fishing by Americans going on there. The instructions issued to Major Moodie were published at the time. They left in the month of September. They wintered at Fullerton bay-We received some letters and information from them by land during the month of April. The information that we received from Major Moodie was to the effect that some of the men would have to come back.
Nobodv had died, but some of the men were sick, some were unfit for service and a certain number of mounted policemen would have to be sent out to relieve them. In order to carry out the plan which was adopted by parliament another boat will have to be sent up there to take in coal and provisions as well as the men who are required to replace those who will have to be brought back I think, after all, the best mode of asserting the authority of Canada ju Hudson bay is bv establishing posts in different places under resident officers of the government and by having our organization completed as much as possible with due regard ir. the via-iit of the people who may be up
there.

What has been the experience in regard to the navigability of Hudson bay and Hudson straits? I saw some time ago in some of the papers that the conditions had been found to be much more favourable than had been anticipated.

They were not specially charged with that because there is in some departments of the government a report made some years ago by Captain Wakeham who was sent specially to ascertain the possibility of navigating the bay and the straits and the length of the season of navigation. I have not the report before me, but_I know there was such a report made about five years ago, and there was also the report of Lieutenant Gordon made in 1881.
Is this expedition not charged with the duty of making observations as to that?

Yes, they are charged with the duty of making observations and of obtaining all the information possible. We have no report yet as to that specially, because all we have received are some letters making urgent demands and not going into details.
(Mr. INGRAM. How many officers are employed in connection with the ' Neptune' ?
There are none.
No officers ?

There is no ' Neptune.' There was one sent up, but she has returned. That was the boat obtained in Newfoundland which was sent up there previously to the purchase of the ' Arctic ' to explore the northern part of Hudson bay. She was under the command of Mr. Low whose report is to be found at page 116 of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
I have here quite a lengthy report signed by A. P. Low.
Yes.
This expedition appears to have taken place in the summer of 1903.
Yes, that was the first expedition that was sent up.
Exactly, and he speaks of some small repairs to this boat. I understood the hon. minister to say that there were very extensive repairs made to this boat. '
They were found to be extensive afterwards when they put her on the slip.

I know they put her on the slip, but it says here that the repairs were very .small.
The ship was immediately placed in dry dock at St. John, where a few small repairs were Mr. PREFONTAINE.
made to her underbody, after which she was speedily sent to Halifax, arriving ihere on the 20th.
That would indicate that the repairs were very small.
That was before she sailed. The repairs to which I have reference were made at Halifax after Mr. Low had left the boat, I think.

There was an item in one of the newspapers-I thought that I could put my hand upon it, but as I cannot do so 1 will have to trust to my memory in quoting -which appeared within the last day or two intimating that Mr. Low had refused to go to the north because the department would not give him the ' Neptune.'
The hon. gentleman refers to something which appeared within the last few days ?
Yes.	'

There was a misapprehension. The papers were mis-informed. We do not intend to send anybody this year to do the work which we suppose the ' Arctjc ' will do. The ' Arctic ' will have two seasons yet to patrol Hudson bay, this season and next year so that we thought there was no reason to send out the ' Neptune ' this year to go over the same ground the ' Arctic ' will go over. We will satisfy ourselves with sending simply an ordinary freight boat which we will hire, to carry the men that we are going to send to the ' Arctic ' and the necessary supplies of coal, &c. That is what created the impression that Mr. Low has refused to go except in the ' Neptune.' We do not ask Mr. Low to go with any other boat, but we are not sending the * Neptune ' so that Mr. Low cannot go. We have the steamship ' Arctic ' there already and so there is no necessity to send another similar boat.
Is there any truth in the statement that Mr. Low considered it was not safe to take his crew in the boat the department wanted to give him ?

Mr. Low is not asked to take any crew, because the ' Neptune ' has her own crew, and she is a rather expensive boat. As there was no necessity for exploring the same waters the ' Arctic ' is going to explore next season and the season following, we thought it would be a saving to send a freight boat with its own captain and its own crew. In that way Mr. Low will not go.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What boat are you getting ?
We have not decided ; we are asking for prices.

Is it true that the department, on the advice of the hon. member for

Halifax (Mr. Roche), has decided to charter the ' Havana ' ?

There is no such decision.* We have asked Captain Patterson his charter price for the ' Havana ' for freight purposes, and he made a proposition which is not satisfactory. He wanted to charter the boat at so much a day, and we wanted to rent her for the round trip. We have not closed yet with Captain Patterson.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is he the only gentleman you inquired from ?
We have inquired everywhere in Canada.
Do we understand that the ' Havana ' is the only boat asked to give a price ?

No ; we have been inquiring for two months for prices in order to send a boat up there. We want a boat to carry supplies to meet the ' Arctic ' and come back. It is not for an expedition, and we consider that the ' Neptune ' is too expensive for that work. We may be obliged yet to take the ' Neptune ' if we cannot get any other in Canada, but any way there is nothing decided.

Then it is purely a departmental affair, and it is not within the power of any members of the administration as a piece of patronage ?
Mr. PRE-FONTAINE. Not a bit of it. We try to get a Canadian vessel.
